SIMULTANEOUS COMMITTEE MEETINGS-DELAY IN PRINTING COMMITTEE PROCEEDINGS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. It is a very serious one which affects all hon. members and the administration of the committees of the House. I bring this matter to the House Leader's attention through you, Mr. Speaker. For example, this morning the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs was sitting at the same time as the Special Committee on the Constitution. Some hon. members are members of both committees, and it was impossible for them to attend both committee meetings because it is impossible for one to be in two places at the same time. We on this side of the House have heard criticisms from various sources that we are not the most effective opposition.

maintopic: SIMULTANEOUS COMMITTEE MEETINGS-DELAY IN PRINTING COMMITTEE PROCEEDINGS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

maintopic: SIMULTANEOUS COMMITTEE MEETINGS-DELAY IN PRINTING COMMITTEE PROCEEDINGS
speechtext:
I am pleased to see that some hon. members who are suffering from similar difficulties with respect to committees approve of what I am saying. But there have been criticisms of that kind.
This government has always stood on words and phrases like "dialogue" and "viable force". How can one carry on a dialogue if one is supposed to be in two different places at the same time? How can we carry out our functions as Members of Parliament if the administration of the House is to be carried on in this fashion?
I draw your attention to something else, Mr. Speaker. The situation is even worse this afternoon. The Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections is to sit at the same time as the Committee of the Whole House will be considering a matter of concern to the members of the standing committee. The personnel of both committees is in part the same, and committees dealing with the same subject will

May 28, 1970
Committee Proceedings be sitting in two different places. No wonder the image of this place is such that the people of the country think it is a lit-up cemetery.

maintopic: SIMULTANEOUS COMMITTEE MEETINGS-DELAY IN PRINTING COMMITTEE PROCEEDINGS
speechtext: Oh, oh!

maintopic: SIMULTANEOUS COMMITTEE MEETINGS-DELAY IN PRINTING COMMITTEE PROCEEDINGS
speechtext: I am raising a serious point, and I hope Your Honour will bear with me because I will not be long. We cannot do our work and create an image of this institution as a viable force if we have to be in ten places at the same time. When the government was in opposition the standing committees were not entrusted with the function of dealing with legislation in the way they now do. They merely studied bills which then came back for further study in the House. I recall that when the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) was Prime Minister the opposition of that day refused to allow the committees to sit while the House was sitting. What is goose for the gander-

maintopic: SIMULTANEOUS COMMITTEE MEETINGS-DELAY IN PRINTING COMMITTEE PROCEEDINGS
speechtext: Oh, oh!

maintopic: SIMULTANEOUS COMMITTEE MEETINGS-DELAY IN PRINTING COMMITTEE PROCEEDINGS
speechtext: What is sauce for the goose is sauce for the gander. Perhaps the phrase I first used explains what has been happening to this institution. There should be some direction in our affairs and the House Leader ought to pay some attention to this aspect of our operations because right now the operations of this institution are a mess. We cannot perform our tasks.

maintopic: SIMULTANEOUS COMMITTEE MEETINGS-DELAY IN PRINTING COMMITTEE PROCEEDINGS

maintopic: SIMULTANEOUS COMMITTEE MEETINGS-DELAY IN PRINTING COMMITTEE PROCEEDINGS
speechtext: On a point of order, Mr. Speaker-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: SIMULTANEOUS COMMITTEE MEETINGS-DELAY IN PRINTING COMMITTEE PROCEEDINGS
speechtext: Order, please. I hope we do not spend the afternoon on a point of order. I see quite a few hon. members who apparently want to take part in the discussion. I doubt very much whether we should get involved in a general discussion on the point of order, important though it is, raised by the hon. member for Calgary North. For the moment the Chair will recognize the hon. member for York South.

maintopic: SIMULTANEOUS COMMITTEE MEETINGS-DELAY IN PRINTING COMMITTEE PROCEEDINGS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, without laying blame on anyone and without entering into the particular matter which was raised this afternoon, I wish to suggest to the House that there is a very real and serious problem with regard to committee meetings.
There is a large number of committees. They meet very frequently. There are many overlaps in the personnel of committees. Frequently a standing committee meets at the same time that the subject with which it is dealing is before the House. The members of the standing committee representing the various parties are obviously the people most concerned with the subject matter being debated on the floor of the House.
I wish to raise again for consideration by Your Honour, members of the House and the House Leaders of all parties something that members of my party have suggested on a number of occasions. We should organize our parliamentary work so that at least on one day a week the House would not sit and the committees would be busy.

maintopic: SIMULTANEOUS COMMITTEE MEETINGS-DELAY IN PRINTING COMMITTEE PROCEEDINGS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

maintopic: SIMULTANEOUS COMMITTEE MEETINGS-DELAY IN PRINTING COMMITTEE PROCEEDINGS
speechtext:
In this way we could avoid this terrible timetable of rushing from one committee to another or from a committee to the House of Commons.
I have known committees to sit for an hour without a quorum. I have known them to start hearing evidence with only two or three members present. They have sometimes spent an hour or an hour and a half waiting for a
May 28, 1970

quorum in order that matters which had been discussed could be dealt with as motions of the committee. Then a quorum is reached at the last minute and members vote without having heard the discussion or in effect knowing what the matter is about. This is an inefficient and ineffective way of carrying on the business of this Parliament.
In saying that, it is not my purpose to lay the blame on the Government House Leader or on anyone else. I suggest that we ought to arrange the work of the House so that on at least one day a week the House will not sit, perhaps on occasion on two days a week. The committees could then do their work without the burden and the inefficiency which are now present.

maintopic: SIMULTANEOUS COMMITTEE MEETINGS-DELAY IN PRINTING COMMITTEE PROCEEDINGS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

maintopic: SIMULTANEOUS COMMITTEE MEETINGS-DELAY IN PRINTING COMMITTEE PROCEEDINGS
speechtext:
I rise on a point of order, Mr. Speaker, related to the point of order of the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Woolliams) with regard to committee operations. I wish to point out to Your Honour, the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Macdonald) and the House one serious problem with which the committees are faced. I do not blame anyone, but I hope a solution can be found to the problem.
The committees are sitting continuously. They have to make reports on their findings following their studies of given matters. However, the printing of the committee proceedings is running over a month behind. The last report we have of the Standing Committee on Agriculture covers the proceedings of a month ago today. The last report we have of the Standing Committee on Transportation covers proceedings of over a month ago. These committees are trying to draft reports based on the studies they have made. I understand that the situation with regard to the finance committee is just as bad. I suggest that the government should take notice of this problem. In light of the serious unemployment throughout the country, possibly some students could be hired so that the printing could be brought more up to date than at present.
Committees cannot deal with the legislation they have studied. They cannot present reports on the problems they are studying. I urge the government to take note of this problem and, if necessary, make use of job printing so that the job can be done. In this way the committees could present worthwhile, thorough and comprehensive reports on which the House could act.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, your suggestion that representatives of all parties discuss the problem of committees is an interesting one. For our part, we approve of it heartily and wish to assure the House of our utmost co-operation.
I rose to indicate that we endorse fully the remarks of the hon. member for York South (Mr. Lewis) to the effect that committees should be given a chance to operate in a more efficient way. Mr. Speaker, we Creditistes are every day subjected to serious discrimination because of the way our committee system operates at the present time.
Due to the great number of government and Conservative members, these two parties have no difficulty in ensuring representation on the committees. Now since we are only 13

May 28, 1970
Committee Proceedings members-we will soon be 14-and as there are more committees than members our group, that means that each of us would have to sit on two or three committees, and that because of an obvious lack of co-ordination in the present committee system. Although each member of the Ralliement creditiste is eager to play an efficient role in committees, he cannot indeed sit on two or three committees at the same time.
Mr. Speaker, we want to request publicly that each hon. member be automatically entitled to appoint a replacement so that, in case of conflicting engagements, the replacement could sit on the committee and enjoy the same privileges and rights as the member he represents, that is, the right to speak and, above all, the right to vote. I consider that this suggestion is positive and important.
The New Democratic party and the Ralliement creditiste seem to suffer discrimination each day and the government, as it is always talking about participation, should take upon itself to accept this proposal.
We want to object to the present system and to invite the representatives of the different parties to positively and seriously study our suggestion at forthcoming meetings.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: SIMULTANEOUS COMMITTEE MEETINGS-DELAY IN PRINTING COMMITTEE PROCEEDINGS
speechtext:
Obviously it will be judged from the contribution made by the hon. member for Lotbiniere that we are now getting into a discussion of a substantive nature on the question. A point of order has been raised. The objections made by hon. members have been noted.
Perhaps I should refer to the fact that some objection has been made by the hon. member for Crowfoot in connection with the printing of documents. If there has been something lacking there, I am sure it is a matter which should be looked into by the Chair and by the officers at the table, and perhaps also in consultation with the Committee on Procedure and Organization.
This having been said, I respectfully suggest to hon. members that we leave the matter at that for the moment, because if we do embark on further discussion we will be having a general debate and, as I have said, I do not think this should be done without a substantive motion being before the House. I will take into due account the points made by hon. members, and perhaps we will have an opportunity very soon to hear representations

from other hon. members, who obviously feel as strongly as the two hon. members who raised these points feel. For the moment the Chair suggests to hon. members that we go on with the business of the House.

Mr. Speaker, I think it is a well recognized fact that Parliament is only as effective as the people who are elected to this chamber. In order that the best people will be elected, we must do everything we can to remove as many of the difficulties as possible which normally stand in the way of good candidates being elected, particularly those who are young and do not have too much of this world's goods with which to finance an election campaign.
One of the main obstacles today is the very high cost of conducting a campaign as a result of the increased use of that very costly medium, television, the increased use of radio, direct mail, billboards and other costly means of advertising both the candidate and his platform. Some years ago the United Kingdom overcame this difficulty by imposing a strict limit on the amount of money a candidate could spend in his riding during an election campaign. By enforcing that restriction, and supervising carefully the expenditures made by each candidate during an election, the election of a candidate could be nullified if it could be proved that he exceeded the funds he was legally allowed to spend.
The amount of the allowable expenditure was worked out according to the number of voters in the riding. When I covered the British election in 1950, the amount allowed was 11 pence per voter in a riding, which was roughly three cents in Canadian currency at that time. I do not know what figure is allowed in Great Britain today, but if we allow for the inflation that has taken place in all countries during the intervening 20 years, I believe it would be safe to assume that it would be in the vicinity of 10 cents per voter in Canadian currency.
This system, which has worked so well in Great Britain, would work equally well in Canada. If we limit the expenditures of a candidate to 10 cents per voter in his riding, we will cut the cost of an election in the average size riding in Canada to approximately $4,000 per candidate. I think every member of this House agrees that this would be a very sizeable reduction in election expenditures in the majority of ridings in Canada. If we do this, we will accomplish two important improvements.

The first will be to make it possible for a potential candidate to stand for his party's nomination irrespective of his personal means. He could count on receiving a great deal or all of the money required from his party or his supporters who always rally round a candidate at election time and contribute to his election expenses. The second accomplishment would be that a candidate would be required to do a great deal more personal campaigning than is usually the case today.
[DOT] (3:20 p.m.)
This has been the case in Great Britain ever since this regulation I have described was brought into force. Most of the means of campaigning which money makes available in Canada and other countries are not open to candidates in Great Britain. Candidates have no choice but to do a great deal of personal campaigning. The same would be true in Canada if we adopted this plan. This would be a tremendous step forward towards ensuring that the best people are elected to Parliament. If a strict limitation of expenditures were imposed on all candidates, the candidates would have no choice but to do a great deal of personal campaigning, calling door to door, going to a great many meetings, presenting their views and submitting to questions. When any of us campaign door to door we submit ourselves to questions by the people in each house. This is very useful and constructive.
Such a regulation would also mean that candidates could not wait until an election is called to take a nomination. If a candidate is going to cover his riding very carefully by personal campaigning, it is necessary to do what candidates in Great Britain have been doing for many years. In Great Britain, candidates are nominated many months, and in some cases several years, before an election is due. They spend a great deal of time getting around the riding, meeting the people, discussing their views with them and expressing their opinion on behalf of a particular party in the next election. They learn what the people in that riding want them to do in Parliament if elected to represent them. It would also enable the voters in a constituency to judge the quality of the candidates far more accurately than is the case today, resulting in a far greater likelihood that the best candidate would be elected on election night.
This would, of course, in turn improve the quality of Parliament; it would improve the quality of those available to be chosen to be members of the cabinet to run the country, 
and this, naturally, would be of tremendous benefit to the country as a whole. It would also make it impossible in the future for a rich man literally to buy his way into Parliament by hiring extensive public relations staff and spending a great deal of money on radio and television time during which he may read speeches which he may not have written and which, indeed, he may not even understand. In fact, he may not be the best man standing in that constituency.
I should like to suggest another change in our election procedure, one which would both reduce the cost of elections and improve the quality of the presentation by the candidate and the party. I believe the length of the campaign should be cut from its present eight weeks to four. The eight week campaign was devised many years ago in the days when the principal means of transportation over long distances was by rail. Eight weeks was required for the party leaders to travel round the country and discuss the issues of the day in all parts of Canada. Today, jet travel and television enable these issues to be discussed in all parts of the country in a maximum of four weeks. Usually, after a campaign has been under way for about three weeks the leaders run out of new issues, and from then on it is a matter of rehashing things that have been said over and over again until the public becomes tired of the campaign.
I believe the initial expenditure needed to maintain a permanent voters' list would be worthwhile. It would make our elections less costly and more interesting. The attention of voters would be attracted more positively than is the case today. Better candidates would be chosen to become Members of Parliament and this would result in the country getting the benefit of better government.

Mr. Speaker, I am delighted to be able to take part in this debate, in which I have been preceded by a number of members who served with me on the Committee on Privileges and Elections which began a review of the Elections Act early last session.
At the outset, I wish to echo the remarks of those who testified that the work of the Committee was carried out on a very dignified and non-partisan plane. Even in our travels, when we went east to discuss certain questions with election officials in New Brunswick, Nova Scotia and Quebec, once a small problem as to whether or not the committee ought to be travelling had been settled, the
May 28, 1870

work of the committee was carried out on a very high plane throughout. I echo the commendation which has been put forward by hon. members opposite with respect to the calibre of the committee and also with respect to the fine work of the chairman.
Anyone who has been through an election campaign, and of course this includes all members of this House, is keenly aware of the glaring weaknesses in our electoral process. Many hon. members have been through more than one campaign, not all of them successful. I can include myself among that number. Not only have I been through more than one campaign, one successful and one unsuccessful, but the one which did not succeed was the subject of a recount. I must say I found this an enlightening experience and worthwhile background for my tour of duty with the committee. Examining carefully, ballot by ballot, the votes which had been cast one could not help but learn a good deal about the difficulties faced by electors when seeking to exercise their franchise accurately and freely.
One might list the weaknesses which were most obvious to members of the committee. They were connected, first, with inaccurate registration of voters; second, with the marking of ballots; third, with the question of party identification; fourth, with the age of voters. Perhaps this should be a general classification covering the ability or disability of a person seeking to exercise a franchise whether because of infirmity, or illness, or age; one could include in this category the question of eligibility by virtue of citizenship as opposed to residence. These were the questions which were in the forefront of the minds of all members of the committee following their experience at the polls.
There is a further consideration, and in this respect I declare my interest as being more aggressive than that of others on the committee. I refer to the opening of liquor outlets on election day. I admit this does not rank in importance with the other considerations I have listed, but I made it clear in my contribution to the committee deliberations that the law which keeps liquor outlets closed is another example of our antiquated thinking on this question. The proposal, now, is that liquor outlets should remain closed only during voting hours instead of all day, as formerly. We have long reached the stage at which resort to alcoholic beverages for social reasons has become a way of life throughout the world. Attempts to restrict the availability of
Canada Elections Act
alcohol ought to have been discarded long ago, not only with respect to election day, but other occasions. I refer to all kinds of restriction, such as restricted hours, the restrictive licensing of premises, restricted hours of sale, and so on. These, I maintain, are vestiges of antiquity which ought to have disappeared. We have prescribed by law that an employee should be entitled to a certain number of hours off duty to ensure that he may exercise his franchise; the motion that the pub might be more attractive to him than the polling booth is one that we ought to shed. Therefore,
I maintain there should be no change made in the status of hours of licensed premises on election day, because I do not think they are a factor at all in the voting process. In any case, we have settled upon what I consider to be a compromise, opening the doors after the polls close, and I welcome at least that development.
[DOT] (3:30 p.m.)
Going back to my list with regard to inaccurate registration, I doubt that anyone opposes in principle the view that has been taken by so many members respecting a permanent electoral list. This would be a great idea. It works in many countries; certainly, it seems to work in Australia. However, the salient difference is that registration for voter identification is compulsory, as is, theoretically at least, the casting of a ballot in that country. I do not find myself opposed in principle to that kind of system. If we had it here, certainly a permanent electoral list would be much more feasible.
However, we have not yet progressed to that stage. The subject of compulsory registration for voting is one of immense proportion from the constitutional point of view, from the point of view of civil liberties, from the point of view of emotions, freedom and so on. I am sure it is something that we will debate at some other time, but I believe that unless we do adopt some kind of system like that a permanent electoral list is not possible in this country.
First of all, think of the formidable expense involved. In addition, Canada is a large country and we do so much to encourage mobility among our people. We already have government programs underway which endorse and subsidize movement across the country of people who are unemployed for various reasons. Through our immigration and manpower policies, we attempt to encourage people to move to different parts

Canada Elections Act
of the country. As I say, Canada is a vast land, a developing nation, and immigration and rapid expansion of the population is encouraged. In this kind of atmosphere any attempt to have permanent registration of voters or a permanent electoral list would not only be expensive but I suggest unrealistic.
Short of that, I welcome and endorse these changes in the electoral law to clarify what are the proper functions of the enumerators and the election officials. I also welcome the new methods by which certain clerical errors and oversights can be corrected in the electoral list, particularly the changes that enable voters to present themselves and obtain a certificate if they have been enumerated but by error have been left off the list.
Too frequently are we caught in a sort of political byplay when we find, through enumeration errors or clerical errors in the process of establishing voter's lists, that certain people have been left off. In such a situation we have fallen into the game of having political workers of all parties taking to the streets early in the campaign, covering their particular area and attempting to find people who have been left off the lists, and triumphantly bringing them before the revising officer and getting them restored to the list. By that act alone, they supposedly win a supporter for their particular candidate.
This is not the way that we should do our electioneering. I think that we do this country a great service when we try to eliminate these kinds of errors, when we try to widen as much as possible the powers of officials to restore to the list people who have been left off through no fault of their own. I think this sort of system should be made as flexible as possible in order to avoid anyone being disenfranchised through no fault of his own. I take pride in the amendments, as far as they go, and some day I hope we will feel that we have completely overcome our problems.
With regard to the marking of ballots, here experience and the opportunity for recount is of particular value. One has only to examine a series of ballots in any election to find that we are required to adhere to the practice of using the marking pencil that is provided in the polling booth. Not only that, but we are required to mark an "X", formed by two lines intersecting diagonally, which is placed beside the name of the candidate in a little box.
Although we were enforcing the letter of the law, we were running contrary to the spirit. There is no doubt that the original 
intention of the legislation was to make it impossible for a person to demonstrate that he had cast his ballot in favour of a certain candidate, for the obvious reason that this would prevent him from being able to sell his vote. In other words, if he were able to prove that he had marked his ballot in a certain fashion, he could be effectively rewarded for having cast his vote for a particular candidate.
Experience has taught us, I am sure, that the onus in this matter was badly misplaced; that we were approaching the problem in the wrong way by saying that we must assume that, unless the law has been complied with in every technical detail, the ballot is spoiled. By the simple change that is made to the wording, we have shifted the onus in this sense. We have shifted our approach and have come about it in precisely the opposite way, which I submit is a very laudable change and is definitely progress. We now say-I certainly hope the judiciary will accept this line of thinking when deliberating over a recount-that unless there is clear indication that the voter is attempting to identify his ballot by means of a very peculiar mark, or is using a type of writing instrument by which he can clearly claim to identify himself, we are going to assume that his ballot has been properly marked.
I suggest that this is a much more appropriate approach to the problem. In order to give weight to that, we have proposed a changed form of ballot with a circle beside the name. Reference has been made to the fact that this idea originated in Belgium. There, the idea was that no specific mark should be placed in the circle opposite the candidate's name but the circle was to be shaded in by the voter. I think this would probably be preferable, but we have at least done quite a bit by providing that no ballot is spoilt because the mark takes a certain form. We are letting in any kind of mark made by a pencil or ball point pen, so long as it does not display some sort of identification.
Along with that is the question of party identification on the ballot. I do not know whether my constituency is typical, but in Sudbury we have a very wide representation of people of ethnic origin other than French and English. I have found that these people have two characteristics pertaining to party identification which are quite significant and important to them. The first, found mostly among the senior citizens in the ethnic
May 28, 1970

groups, is a strong sense of party loyalty. Whether one argues that this is a laudable or a lamentable aspect of their approach to politics, I do not know, but it is nevertheless the privilege of any citizen of Canada to be fiercely loyal to a particular party. I have found people of ethnic origin other than French or Anglo-Saxon are not only fiercely loyal to the party of their choice, but tend to remain so throughout their lives. Therefore, the question of party identification is extremely important to them.
In addition to that, the first generation immigrants to this country have difficulty in reading and understanding much of the election material that is circulated to them, as well as the advertising material they hear over television and radio. Therefore, frequently when they go to the polls they are very confused because they are not able to determine or to ask somebody in the poll which candidate on the ballot represents the Liberal party, the Conservative party, or the New Democratic party, as the case may be. For those people alone, if not for the nation as a whole, it is a great advance to place identification by party affiliation of the particular candidates on the ballot papers. I also think it is a great advance to replace the address and occupation of the candidates with their party affiliation.
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)
Much has been said about the importance of political parties in the democratic process. Here again, the debate could rage on and on but, being as non-partisan as we can about the subject of politics, I think we must agree that if the political party functions properly it is the key instrument in the democratic process in our country. It is important, therefore, that this connection with our democratic and representative process be strengthened by the placing of the party identification on the ballot. In addition to that, however, I say it is more important to have the party affiliation on the ballot than to have the profession of the candidate.
Another reason I believe it is more important to have the party affiliation on the ballot than it is to have the profession is that often the description of the profession of a candidate is something which absolutely challenges the imagination of the public relations and advertising people. There have been legendary stories concerning the chosen occupations and there are certain members of this House who could regale other members concerning
Canada Elections Act
the manner in which they described their occupation on the ballot and the reason they adopted that particular description of their profession. I think showing the party affiliation on the ballot will better enable the elector to cast his ballot for the party of his choice.
On the subject of the reduction of the voting age to age 18, much has been said. There was scarcely any discernible disagreement in the committee. Some members expressed concern that the youth vote was a dangerous thing and that there would be a concerted movement among people between ages 18 and 21. I think it has been demonstrated that this fear is ill founded. Past election results in areas where the voting privilege has been extended to people of 18 years of age have shown that the pattern in the age group 18 to 21 is very similar to the pattern in the group over 21 years of age. Therefore, I do not think there is any well-grounded fear in this regard.
I also observe that those who have this fear believe that candidates of 18 years of age would be proposed and emphatically supported en bloc by people 18, 19 and 20 years of age. I have not noticed, and I would invite other members of the House to relate when they have noticed, that any group in the ages 21, 22 and 23, in Canada or in other parts of the world, have united to elect a 21 year old candidate. I do not believe there has been a concerted effort by persons between age 21 and age 25 to nominate and elect their own candidate. I think when there has been action by people in the age group between 21 and 23 it has been through the process of the party system. This is another aspect of the importance of the party system. I do not think there has been an important trend towards the nomination of young candidates in cases where the franchise age has been lowered to 18.
The question of the party system comes up again here. I think everyone will agree there is a definite advantage in being the official candidate of one of the recognized parties when seeking election to this House. Certainly, in the last general election no independent candidate was elected.

speechtext: rise on a point of order. There was one independent candidate elected at the last election. He is the Speaker of the present House.

Far be it from me to be one of those who would ever question the independence of the speaker. It was my impression,

Canada Elections Act
however, that at one time Your Honour was among the ranks of one of the recognized parties. Please forgive my oversight. Also I gather there is a certain advantage, no matter in what capacity, to run unopposed.
He was.

I think we can consider that to be something of a unique situation. Obviously, there is an advantage in being the official candidate of a recognized party. That being the case, one has to consider the possibility of
18	year old or 19 year old candidates being nominated. In principle, there is nothing the matter with an 18 year old or a 19 year old being nominated. If indeed an 18 year old or
19	year old who had intelligence, energy and responsibility were nominated and elected, I would be the first to welcome him to this chamber. On many occasions I have said that the relevance of what happens in this chamber in the eyes of the public is a very vital issue. When we pass into history, one of the issues upon which we will be judged will be whether or not we insured that the public would continue to believe our actions in this chamber are relevant because the young people of our country, as I have said during rules debates and on other occasions, have a very clear choice. Certainly, they intend and want to change the old order. God bless them for that. But their choice is whether they want to change the old order through their own efforts within the existing system or through more revolutionary methods. I say it is vital to encourage them to come here and participate in this and other institutions of our government. In this way we will make sure they have an opportunity to make a very effective contribution which will satisfy them this is the kind of place in which they would be proud to participate. In other words, they will be satisfied it is a very relevant and dynamic institution. I feel that lowering the voting age to 18 to include those people in our electoral process, as well as making them eligible to come here and participate, is a step in the right direction.
On the question of eligibility, may I say that I come from a constituency with a very high incidence of people who emigrated to this country from Europe who are of neither French nor Anglo-Saxon origin. I have always been very sensitive indeed concerning these people. In my experience with and exposure to them, I find these immigrant people who come to our country take their responsibilities as citizens extremely seriously. We have

among them the type of people who helped build this nation. Although they may be humble, quiet and not active in public affairs, we find among them the kind of fibre we want in order to build this nation. The preference in respect of people who come from the British Isles or other Commonwealth countries, who are not required to become citizens of the country in order to vote while immigrants from other countries are required to do so, is something about which I have always been very sensitive. I am glad to see that this is to be changed and these British subjects, if they wish to participate actively in the political life of our country, will have to apply for and obtain citizenship. I believe that is proper.
The move towards the proxy vote I think is a very daring one. We have moved into an area in which I can scarcely blame those who are fearful about abuses of this political process. This is a system in which, unless there are safeguards, there could be very wide abuses. To begin with, Mr. Speaker, we have built into this legislation the necessary safeguards, providing they are watched and regulated by a very careful organization under the guidance and direction of the Chief Electoral Officer. In addition, with those safeguards built in, I feel that the purpose is extremely worthwhile. All of us who have run for office have been sensitive to the fact that many people in hospital and otherwise disabled, and many people in certain occupations, through no fault of their own have been unable to cast their ballots. Every effort is made by the electoral officer to reach these people with a ballot box, but there are certain very severe limitations. It is impossible to fit the law into every little corner of our society, but by embracing a proxy system, very strictly controlled, we tend to extend the privilege of exercising the franchise, and we get into a great many corners that previously we were unable to reach. I embrace that as a very progressive step, provided we rigidly control it. I see in this system an opportunity for a great many people, who would otherwise be unable to cast their ballots, to cast their ballots. I think that is a laudable step.
[DOT] (3:50 p.m.)
When we sum it all up, what we are trying to do is to see to it that the election result is a true expression of the will of the people. That means that all of those people who want to vote have an opportunity to do so, that they are able to cast their ballots in freedom, and
May 28, 1970

that they are able to the greatest degree to understand the requirements for becoming eligible to vote.
We have attempted to clarify our election law, and we have up-dated the language in certain sections. By these amendments I have spoken about, we have attempted to sweep away some of the inequities that existed in the past. This new act will be a compendium of all election rules and regulations so that anyone who wishes may examine them all in one place at one time.
We have done a great deal of work on the provisions for the registration of the voter and the process whereby the voter casts his ballot. We have done almost all that has to be done in that area, but I feel very strongly that a great deal still remains to be done on the other side of the process, that is to say, the selection, or eligibility, or availability of candidates who seek membership in this House. I know that it is somewhat self-serving and suspect when I refer to recent amendments made by the House to the members' pension plan, amendments which have been so widely criticized in the press. But be that as it may, it is a move which is taking away some of the risk from seeking membership in this House. There are a great many lawyers, and I am one, who are members of the House. It is no surprise that this is so. Aside from the fact that lawyers are close to the political process as a result of their study of the law, the fact is that there is less risk for lawyers to make themselves available for an election campaign, than there is for people in other walks of life. It is more advantageous for lawyers to seek membership in this House, and moreover there is less financial risk for them in doing so. They can accommodate their business here with their own personal practice more easily than can many other citizens. That is an inequity. It is an advantage which falls to lawyers, and which is a weakness in our system.
We have done a great deal when we remove the financial risk for people in other walks of life, such as teachers and merchants, engineers and craftsmen, persons in occupations of that sort, who seek membership in this House and who do not have the flexibility to maintain contact with the practice of their professions while here. These people would suffer from being out of contact with their professions because they would miss the new technology, the new terminology and the new ideas being developed in their own fields. When we take any step in the direction of
Canada Elections Act
making it easier for such people to come here, then we are moving in the right direction and are doing a good thing.
When we have taken out the financial risks to the greatest degree possible, and have made it more feasible for those people to come here, the next thing we have to tackle is the question of election expenses. We have to develop a system like that which is in vogue in some provinces and some countries whereby candidates are subsidized to such a degree as to enable them to carry out sensible and vigorous campaigns. If funds are made available to them from government sources they will not have to rely on private contributions, on financial support which is available to some but not to others. This is a situation which makes it difficult for people in certain lines of work, or in certain professions, who lack contact with the business world. Such people have more difficulty in making the plunge into politics.
Associated with this is the question of party affiliations on the ballot. When we are dealing with the question of party affiliations on the ballot we could talk all afternoon about the number of candidates that a party should nominate in order to qualify for party affiliation to be shown. In committee we said we should make it such a number that a frivolous group could not get on the ballot, but at the same time we should not place the number so high as to place a genuine impediment in the way of organizations which wish, in good faith, to become established as political parties. We talked about figures from 25 to 100, and now the government has recommended the figure of 75. I think the exact number of 75 with respect to placing party affiliation on the ballot is not nearly as important as it will be when we come to deal with the question of financial support for candidates running in national elections.
When we discuss the question of eligibility for subsidization by the government to cover election expenses, I think we have to be fairly careful to stipulate a high number of candidates for any party. I believe that 75 is not an unreasonable number. For all the difference it makes concerning party affiliation on the ballot, I think we should be consistent and fix 75 as the number with respect to government financial support. I, therefore, endorse the number of 75 for the purposes of party affiliation on the ballot, and say the number should be the same when we come to deal with the question of subsidies to cover election expenses.

I feel that in so far as enabling the voter to make his choice freely and accurately is concerned, we have gone as far as we can go under present information and knowledge. I think the committee has done a good job, and much has been accomplished here in clarifying this process and making it easier for the voter to cast his ballot. However, I hope we will do more on the other side to enable candidates to come forward and offer themselves for office. I share the pride, which other hon. members have expressed, in the work done by the committee.
Would the hon. member accept a question?
Indeed.

Regarding the points he made, and the ones I made yesterday about party affiliation on the ballot, that is the argument as between 26 candidates and 75 candidates, would he not agree that there is no good reason, when it comes to the question of election expenses and public funds being provided, why there could not be a differentiation between the number of candidates in the field and the number which is required in order to have party affiliation appear on the ballot?

There is no doubt, Mr. Speaker, that it is possible to have different numbers for these two purposes. I thought a lot about that prior to making my remarks, and I am inclined to think that we should remain consistent with respect to the two. My experience at the polls, and I am sure it is that of the hon. member, is that there is much that seems very clear to us when we are closely associated, as we are as candidates, with the election process, but which is very confusing to people who are not as experienced as we are. It is very easy to create confusion in the minds of the electorate about things of this sort. I am very much inclined to think that if we have one number for the purpose of establishing party affiliation on the ballot, say 25 or 26, and a higher number, say 75, for qualification for election expenses, we are bound to create confusion among some people as to their eligibility for subsidization of election expenses. I think this would be an extremely dangerous thing and I therefore say, purely for purposes of consistency and simplicity, that I endorse the one number.
[DOT] (4:00 p.m.)

May I ask one further question, Mr. Speaker? Does the hon. member not

feel that there is some danger of discrimination against a legitimate and serious group forming a new party, or a party that is presently in existence but not represented in the House, in terms of the privilege of having the party affiliation on the ballot? In such a case does he not foresee that this is discriminatory and works against their right to be a recognized party?

Mr. Speaker, the law is discriminatory in that sense even if it requires ten candidates. If you want to call it discrimination you are only dealing with a degree of it because if you require ten candidates, someone could claim that is being discriminatory and indeed it would be. The number 75 virtually requires that a party be genuinely national. It is possible to field 75 candidates in Ontario or Quebec alone, but it certainly is preferable, when putting a party's name on a ballot, that we encourage it to be a party which expresses national interests and therefore spreads its candidates over as wide an area as possible. That is another reason for going to the number 75. If you stop at 25 or 50, that is discriminatory in a sense, at least in the sense in which the hon. member has put his question. In so far as numbers, are concerned, I think the number 75 is probably as fair as any other.

It may
seem odd, Mr. Speaker, that I should make the nub of my complaint against Bill C-215, which is an immense volume of 355 pages, that it does not contain enough. But the fact is that the bill is more notable for what it leaves out than for what it contains. It is a repair job. What our election law needs is a complete reconstruction. In introducing this bill, the government has shown its unwillingness and its failure to accept the real and genuine reform of our electoral system required to make it truly democratic.
Nearly four years ago the Barbeau committee made its report on election expenses. Distinguished and experienced people from different parties served on that committee, including the Honourable M. J. Coldwell, long a leader of the party I supported. The report proposed a number of practical and fundamental recommendations which, if adopted, would have put an end to the present undemocratic, unjust system of secret and unlimited campaign contributions and expenses.
The bill before us ignores the report. It contains a vast number of small, and perhaps
May 28, 1970

useful, changes in detail in our electoral law. Most of these changes will receive our support, although we have some amendments to present. But what is truly significant is that the major reform is postponed. The President of the Privy Council (Mr. Macdonald) tells us that at some future date a special committee will be set up to study the Barbeau report. What is needed, if this government is serious about electoral reform, is not further study by some committee, whether of this House or some other forum, but legislation implementing the report's recommendations which can then go to the committee.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I wonder if the hon. member will permit a question? Does he realize that the suggestion of having a study of this measure by special committee emanated from the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles)?

I have discussed it with him, Mr. Speaker, and he says he made it long ago and it should have been acted upon. As far as I am concerned, I think the committee should study the matter in the light of draft legislation presented by the government. The basic proposals have been clearly laid down in the committee report.
The failure of the government to do anything about this report to date, nearly four and a half years after it has been issued, after one election has been held and now that Parliament is half way through its normal life and heading in the direction I would say of another election, raises very serious doubts about the sincerity of the government's commitment to the implementation of the report. After the report was published in October, 1966, I put a question to the Prime Minister of the day, Mr. Pearson, asking if the government proposed to implement its recommendations. He replied that the government was studying the report with that in mind, and he indicated that legislation would be drafted and presented to the House.
I had an opportunity to speak to the minister then in charge, the Honourable Judy LaMarsh who was secretary of state at that time. She represented what I would call the hard headed school of politicians under the Liberal party, those who could not have cared less about election reform. She said it would take at least a year for the government to find draftsmen able to produce the legislation in draft form. At the time I offered to do it for her in a month but she would not accept my offer.
Canada Elections Act
For free?

Yes, I would have done it for free. It is now three and a half years later and no draft legislation is available, nor does it look as though any is to be made available.
I wonder if the legislation flowing from this report will be available by the time of the next election? I suggest this is history, and an indication of the government's enthusiasm for electoral reform.
I should like to remind the House of the essence of the Barbeau report. It recited the history of huge, secret campaign contributions from government contractors and other interested parties throughout this country. It recalled the Pacific and Beauharnois scandals which revealed to the public something of the corruption of an electoral and political system which depended for its efficient operation on large, hidden contributions to campaign funds. It recited the weaknesses of all legislative efforts to date to deal with this evil. I should like to read a passage from the report: Even though the device of publicity, which has been at the heart of all the attempts at legislation, has not been effectively realized, the idea should not be dismissed as impractical or meaningless. The fact is that the device of publicity has never been really tested. Two fatal weaknesses have vitiated ail efforts in that direction: the failure to recognize political parties as essential units of political finance, and the failure to provide effective machinery for enforcing the laws. It is not possible at the moment to conclude that publicity has failed, only that it has never been properly tried. Other devices, such as subsidies, limitations, and tax inducements have yet to be explored.
At page 28, Mr. Speaker, the report underlines something which I should like to emphasize, namely, if any democratic government is to be effective it is important to have good legislation on political finances. The report reads:
If we wish to improve the workings of democratic government in Canada, we must have legislation that will suppress any parasitic elements that might weaken democratic mechanisms. At best, campaigning is an expensive business: and if expenses run high, income must be significant.
[DOT] (4:10 p.m.)
The source of income must not be such as to prevent parties and legislators from adopting legislation that is in the public interest. I am abandoning for a moment the rather studied language of the report. It seems to me that the committee is saying that the present system of election financing does not operate in the public interest. I could not agree more

with that statement. We have a distorted, inefficient and unsatisfactory system by reason of this situation in election financing.
We now have too many Grits.

The present system gives undue influence to those corporate interests which alone are able to supply moneys that are required to operate modern election campaigns on a national scale.
We recognize that there is a need for the elector to be informed, if he is to make a simple choice. We realize that if the electorate is to be informed we must use methods which, apart from that most important and secret weapon, individual contact, involve radio, television, newspapers, leaflets, billboards, etc. These all cost money. It is important that the source of these funds, necessary if the electorate is to be informed, should be open and known. These funds should not confer on the donors any special rights or privileges in the process of government. We shall not see a genuine democracy until each Canadian citizen has equal influence on the process of government. That is not so under our present system.
The committee had very little difficulty in finding that "sources of funds for political parties and candidates are shrouded in mystery. ' Those are the words of the committee. The committee makes recommendations, which I shall list in more detail in a minute, to meet this situation. The committee recommends that the state provide a reasonable scale of funds for election expenses, something which ought to be acceptable to those who speak of participatory democracy. It also suggests that individuals should be encouraged to make modest contributions to campaign expenses, and that these contributions ought to be deductible for income tax purposes.
At page 34 of the report, after a number of suggestions have been made, the committee says this:
Should Parliament accept these principles-
Those being the principles enunciated by the committee.
-the parties and candidates will be freed from reliance on special interests, and elected members will be freer to perform their duties in the general interests of the people as a whole.
That puts the case in a nutshell. The committee found that if this principle were not accepted, parties and candidates could not be freed from reliance on special interests. In 
DEBATES	May 28, 1970
other words, elected members and their parties are not as free as they might be to serve the people as a whole. That is the actual situation now facing us, and we must change this by implementing the committee's recommendations.
May I read the last paragraph on page 35? The disclosure of funds and their sources seems to the Committee to be indispensable if the electorate is to have confidence in the democratic system. It is emphasized that with the best legislation in the world nothing will be changed if candidates and their parties do not assume their responsibilities, or are the first to violate the laws. For this reason the Committee has concluded that enforcement of the law must be a specific duty of an administrative agency as suggested in this chapter.
May I again underline the paragraph's first sentence?
The disclosure of funds and their sources seems to the Committee to be indispensable if the electorate is to have confidence in the democratic system.
We live in an age when many people view our institutions with grave doubt. What the committee has found, I suggest, is absolutely true. Unless the source of election funds is made clear, how can we ask our people to display confidence in our democratic system?
I wish to deal with another aspect also. Fears are frequently, and I think justifiably, expressed as to what may happen as a result of the overwhelming penetration in this country of foreign ownership. We are told that economic power may lead to political power. It would be the easiest thing in the world, so long as we preserve the same system of financing our political parties as we now have, for there to be a massive intervention from outside in our affairs through the medium of financial contributions in election campaigns.
I understand the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) wishes to raise a question of privilege. I will therefore gladly yield the floor to him.

speechtext: Order, please. I think we have pursued this as far as I am prepared to allow. I take it that the subject raised by the hon. member for Edmonton West will be discussed by the House leaders.

The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Macdonald (Rosedale) that Bill C-215 respecting the franchise of electors and the election of Members to the House of Commons, be read the second time and referred to committee of the whole.

I wish to make it clear that, although I was willing to have the hon. member intervene for the purpose of a point of privilege, I do not wish it to be a precedent such as is followed in the American Congress where people frequently yield to their colleagues. I do not want to suggest that I am always in such a yielding mood.
I was speaking about the very real threat to Canadian democracy which is incidental in the fact that we have a very large measure of 
foreign ownership of our businesses and corporations. As long as we have an electoral system which permits secrecy in so far as contributions to campaign funds, there exists a very real danger. Without the Canadian people knowing it, contributions can be made by people whose allegiance is not to this country. This provides for the possibility of a very serious undermining of our political independence. I tend to be moderate in my fears and views on this foreign influence. I believe the Canadian people are capable of forming an independent judgment. I am not suggesting that foreign corporations, as long as they are domiciled in this country, should be forbidden from contributing to campaign expenditures, but this should be known by the Canadian people.
It is of the utmost importance that we accept the proposals of the Barbeau Committee, including the recommendation of full publicity and limitation of campaign contributions. There is a political danger which threatens the independence of this country. This should be studied by this government. The government should be prompted to bring in the reforms proposed by the Barbeau Committee at an early date. The reforms proposed by the Barbeau Committee are basic to any fundamental reform of our political system.
Although the proposals of this bill are voluminous, they are peripheral. We do not object to these proposals, although we will be suggesting some changes. This debate should not end without a specific pledge by the government to introduce legislation containing the main recommendations of the Barbeau Committee. I say to the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Macdonald) that if this debate ends without a clear indication from the government along this line, we will know that the government is dragging its feet on serious reform of our electoral system.
Your Honour may be surprised to hear that I have friends within the Liberal party, both outside and inside this House. Usually they speak to me in confidence, but perhaps they would speak openly because they are left wing Liberals. They are reformers at heart. They joined the Liberal party because they believed it was a genuine instrument of reform.
That's what it is.

That is what they told me. They believe that they can effectively advance needed changes in our political and social system. I say to them that here is the
May 28, 1970

acid test: the Barbeau Committee has proposed a detailed, practical and sweeping reform of our present undemocratic system which is biased in favour of the corporate elite. I challenge the government to produce draft legislation to implement this reform. There is no need of another committee study before the legislation is introduced. The committee study can come after the government has decided on the basic principles. I challenge the left wing Liberals and reformers in the Liberal party, if there are any, and the present Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) who used to be counted among them, to make sure that this government means business on this issue of electoral reform and will not come in with some sort of half-baked, inefficient, useless so-called compromise, but with the full recommendation of the committee.
If before the next election the government has not added to the bill now before us, which only deals with detailed repairs to our electoral system, the whole new structure of election finances and expenses proposed by the Barbeau Committee, we shall know how hollow the government's claim is of their belief in reform and genuine democracy.
[DOT] (4:30 p.m.)

Mr. Yves Forest (Parliamentary Secretary
to President of the Privy Council): Mr. Speaker, I had the honour to be on the Committee on Privileges and Elections, which made recommendations for amendments to the Elections Act-recommendations which were for the most part incorporated in this legislation-and I must say that the committee was presided over with tact and efficiency by the hon. member for Montmorency (Mr. La-flamme).
Mr. Speaker, as did many other hon. members, I would like to point out that we received the valuable help of the chief electoral officer, who let us benefit by his experience and advice, a fact that all those who have taken part in this debate so far were pleased to mention.
Mr. Speaker, my speech will not be very long since the main provisions of this bill were explained yesterday by the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Macdonald) as well as by other members of this House. I will merely make a few remarks about the bill before us which deals with the consolidation of the Elections Act.
In reply to the previous speaker who talked only about election expenses, I should like to
Canada Elections Act
point out that this question has been allowed to stand and will soon be the subject of a study by a special committee, according to the suggestion made by a colleague of the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin). Had the government followed his suggestion and introduced a bill on election expenses, it would have been blamed for it because its action would supposedly have been taken without referring the matter to all the members of the committee. I believe the government is quite right in referring this important study to a committee made up of representatives of all parties, that could look into the matter and consider the Barbeau Committee Report which contains some good recommendations while others have to be studied in depth.
Mr. Speaker, we have before us a very important piece of legislation. The Elections Act ensures the operation of a sound democracy and is one of the essential elements of our government system.
When we consider the various procedures in the provinces and in other countries, we come to the conclusion that our Elections Act may not be perfect, but it seems to be the best that could have been passed and the most consistent -with our traditions, our customs and our needs, taking into account the vastness of our country and the mobility of our population.
The committee made recommendations and the bill includes improvements and changes intended to enable the greatest number of qualified citizens to exercise their franchise, a principle members of the committee constantly bore in mind.
For example, by instituting a system of proxy voting for certain classes of persons such as fishermen, mariners, prospectors, persons who because of illness or physical incapacity are confined in hospitals or elsewhere, fulltime students in educational institutions-when the election takes place during an academic term-and public service electors on duty abroad as well as all dependent electors who are dependents of such public service electors, and also by extending the right to vote at advance polls, I believe the new Canada Elections Act fully achieves its objectives, while remaining in the realm of the possible and the practicable, in the absence of a permanent voters' list, which should be necessary to permit the absentees to exercise their franchise.
Mr. Speaker, on several occasions, and mainly at the time of the recent elections in

nated in at least 10 per cent of the electoral districts in Canada on the 28th day before polling day, a necessary delay as that day is nomination day, I believe, in the 21 constituencies listed in Schedule III of the Act.
The government has modified that provision by stipulating, in the bill, that this advantage will be reserved to parties with candidates in 75 electoral districts that is to parties of national standing, and not to those fly-hy-nighters, that sometimes crop up, as in the last election, when a party known as, I believe, the Rhinoceros had several candidates. As the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre (Mr. Benjamin) pointed out himself yesterday, this will be all the more necessary when the matter of reimbursing electoral expenses comes up. I for one do not feel that it is necessarily anti-democratic to require that a party have candidates in just over 25 per cent of the electoral districts in order to be considered as a national party, instead of a minigroup, a local or regional party.
Mr. Speaker, it was also said that in the future the right to vote should be reserved to Canadian citizens only, and the committee was in favour of that idea. But, after long discussions, they agreed that it might be irregular, if not unfair, to deprive of their franchise those who had it in 1968, at the time of the last general election, and who have had it since. The government adopted a similar attitude, but it may be only temporary. There may be changes which might encourage people to ask for their Canadian citizenship.
Mr. Speaker, many other provisions should be discussed, but I do not want to delay any further the passing of this excellent legislation, which will, in any event, be studied in committee. I presume that study will be rather lengthy because of the great number of changes. But, precisely because of those changes, and the increasing publicity which doubtless will be given those amendments and the new provisions in the bill, I trust some progress has been made. The government had committed itself to recasting the Elections Act and I am sure that such a move will be welcomed by the people.

Mr. Speaker, a step by step study of the Elections Act seems to me a sound and relevant way to deal with the overall reform of the legislation.
The minister's decision-supported by all the members of the House-to proceed step by step is therefore most welcome. One 22375-53
Canada Elections Act
cannot expect to complete at one fell swoop and within a few months all the reforms our Elections Act calls for.
It is very wise, for example, to set up a special committee to study in depth and in detail the item dealing with the electoral expenditures.
This study should not, however, be delayed. The expenditures are one of the main hindrances to a true democracy, where, at long last, ideas and opinions would supersede powerful and sometimes nefarious influence of money.
It is therefore imperative that we should all be involved in the cost of elections. This is one way for Canadians to come closer to government by the people.
On this side of the House, we, the Credi-tistes in particular, have always felt the regrettable influence of slush funds which jeopardize the free play of democracy. The sooner is passed a legislation which will control expenditures, the sooner the people will exert a healthy influence on their rulers. It is therefore to be hoped that by the end of 1971 at the latest, this most serious matter will finally be settled.
The arguments put forward by the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Macdonald) with regard to the permanent list of electors, have almost convinced me. If in fact the experience of various countries such as France, England and Australia which already have a permanent list, proves to be quite questionable and ineffective, we should, I agree, think twice before establishing one in this country.
However, I fear that the minister might have let himself be overly influenced by a piece of legislation passed in this House in 1934 and which was immediately repealed in 1938. The vastness of Canada, its widely scattered population, the little information available to a great many of our people in more or less remote areas, all these things do not exist nowadays, due to all the modern facilities brought about by progress.
At first blush, I feel that many more arguments will have to be put forward before we are really convinced that a permanent election list would not be workable. The cost of such a list may seem greater since it would be difficult and expensive to bring it up to date. But, considering the numerous and various uses it could have, perhaps the cost would not be outrageous after all.

May 28, 1970
Canada Elections Act
It is easy enough, for instance, for the Department of National Revenue, to know who is who. There is the census, there are reports from municipalities, parishes, provinces or other offices who keep an eye on the population. A good co-ordination of all those sources of information should be seriously considered. In brief, we should explore every avenue to find out whether it would not be worthwhile considering again the possibility of a permanent election list. If the committee has done this, I shall accept their conclusions.
As far as Canadians voting abroad are concerned, indeed, those whose duties allow them to keep abreast of what goes on in this country deserve to be able to vote. However, I would make some reservations, if not some objections.
I can hardly imagine someone totally unaware of what has been happening in the country for years and who might be told of the government's competence and generosity right before the poll, casting a truly free vote.
Mr. Speaker, I still have fresh in my memory a judicial recount in my constituency, after the last election. Having had the opportunity to see each ballot paper, I noted some peculiarities, for instance, similar handwriting among Canadian forces men, or the name of the candidate appearing on a special ballot paper.
A few weeks later, I met a soldier who told me that, while he was in hospital in Ontario, a returning officer had come to see him and had told him, among other things, that he was to vote in the Champlain riding where there were four candidates, two of which bore the name "Matte". The soldier asked him which one was a Creditiste. The returning officer answered immediately "Jean-Paul Matte", thus giving another vote to the liberal candidate.
There are so many possible ways of circumventing somewhat the democratic process that I wonder if, for a few hundred or a few thousand people, we should risk getting votes that are more or less sincere and reasonable. We should first of all, I think, make every effort to enable someone who is abroad to vote in his riding-thus many votes cast abroad would be rejected-and we should also seriously consider whether it can be truly useful to have ballot boxes travel around the world in a Canadian election.
Even though it may well be understood, I cannot see any difference between a person who works for the government or one who is

self-employed, although the President of the Privy Council seemed to make a case of it in his remarks. I cannot see any difference whether one or the other happens to be away from his usual place of residence or his constituency on election day.
Is it not the same, for instance, if an individual from Champlain riding happens to be in Vancouver during the month of the election or if a person is working for NATO in Europe on behalf of the government?
So naturally I think that a more reasonable method should be found to enable the greatest number of Canadians to vote, but there will always be some who will have to be sacrificed to safeguard true freedom.
In my opinion, this reform of the Elections Act is timely, Mr. Speaker, and I hope that it will be considered with adequate seriousness, so that when the time comes for the people to elect a new government, they will vote themselves power instead of leaving it all to the government. That is democracy, and I believe that the act which regulates elections must safeguard at any cost the basic principle of human freedom.
[DOT] (4:50 p.m.)

Mr. Speaker, time is short today and, therefore, I do not have sufficient time to review even a portion of this very voluminous bill which is before us. I should like, however, to bring to the attention of the House the clause which deals with proxy voting and which represents the committee's resolution of the problem concerning voters who are absent from their places of residence in which they are registered on voting day. In my riding, and in many ridings of the west, northern Canada and portions of eastern Canada, this is a serious problem. After due study of the matter the committee chose the proxy balloting system in preference to the absentee balloting system. I know members of the committee studied this matter long and hard, and the majority came to the conclusion that the absentee balloting system is not workable in federal elections.
I am disturbed to find that the classification of workers who would be given the opportunity to register their vote through a proxy is limited pretty well to fishermen and prospectors. Therefore, it is my intention when this debate reaches the committee of the whole stage to move an amendment in this regard. Certainly, in relation to my own
May 28. 1970

riding and several other ridings of which I am aware in British Columbia, it would be quite improper that loggers not be included in this clause. With my eye on the clock, I thank the House for its attention.
Mr. Speaker, it is close enough to five o'clock to call it five o'clock if the chair would agree.
