AFTER RECESS

The House resumed at 8 p.m.

The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Macdonald (Rosedale) that Bill C-215, respecting the franchise of electors and the election of members to the House of Commons, be read the second time and referred to committee of the whole.

Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to have an opportunity to talk briefly on Bill C-215, the Canada Elections Act. It is a voluminous document. It is enough to frighten members of the House, having 355 pages of subject matter. One might well wonder why so much regulation is needed to rim an election, but on checking through the bill I find that although
May 28, 1970

there are a number of very interesting and good amendments suggested by the government and by the committee which did a great deal of work on the Canada Elections Act prior to the drafting of this document, there are still one or two areas desperately in need of amendment. It is not my intention tonight to go over the entire bill; I felt I would deal with two or three of the major points, points that the government and members of the House should take another look at before finally passing into law the huge bill that is under debate.
The first point I should like to deal with tonight is the problem of getting the vote to those Canadians who are entitled to be on the voters' list. I have been through a number of elections, federal, provincial and municipal, as have most members of this House, and over the years I have come to realize how desperately we have needed electoral change, not only in the federal field but in the provincial and municipal fields.
In going over the report issued by the Chief Electoral Officer following the last election that took place in 1968, a report supplied to all members, I find some very interesting figures that I think hon. members should take into consideration when making changes in respect of the new act. I should like to draw to the attention of members of the House and Canadians generally that in the 1968 federal election 10,860,000 Canadians were on the voters' list. Out of this total, 8,218,000 cast ballots, which means that 2,642,000 Canadians failed to go to the polls for one reason or another. This figure is staggering when you realize that about 24 per cent, or one out of every four Canadians, did not cast a ballot in 1968.
I am not naive enough to think you can devise a system that will provide 100 per cent voter participation. Some countries have compulsory voting. I do not know how successful is a system that forces people who have no interest in an issue to cast a ballot, and I am not sure that this is the solution. But when I think of the 2,642,000 Canadians who did not cast their vote in 1968 I wonder just how efficient we as legislators have been in drafting our Elections Act and setting up election machinery to enable Canadians to cast ballots.
[DOT] (8:10 p.m.)
I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, and to hon. members that people do not cast their ballots for a variety of reasons. Sometimes they are
Canada Elections Act
just not interested. A number of Canadians do not cast their ballots because of religious beliefs. Then we have those people who are incapacitated and thus are unable to go to the polls. I believe we then come to the group which represents the greatest number of Canadians who do not vote: this is the group of electors who are absent from their constituencies on voting day. I should like to say a few words about this group.
I know that in this bill there are one or two minor amendments dealing with proxy voting. This, however, does not cover those Canadians who in this vast country of ours are for one reason or another forced to be absent from their constituencies on voting day. They are deprived of the right to participate in choosing the government of their country. I think this is an important issue because under our system of democracy the most precious thing we have is the right to cast a ballot for the party or program of our choice.
In the world of today we believe we have a good system of choosing representatives whom we wish to be elected. We should enact every measure we can to make certain the electorate of this country has as wide a participation as possible. I feel that one way to achieve this end is to set up an absentee system of voting. I am well aware that the committee studied this problem. I am also well aware of the tremendous difficulty that lies in the way of setting up an adequate absentee voting system in Canada. I say, however, we must devise a system that will allow Canadians who are absent from their constituencies on voting day to cast their ballots by means of absentee vote. I am convinced this can be accomplished if we are willing to spend the money required to set up the proper type of system and give it a try.
Who, primarily, are the people who are absent from their constituencies? It is difficult to pinpoint any particular group or individuals, but the bulk of those who are absent from their constituencies on voting day are involved in occupations which require that they be absent from home. They may be in another part of the province or in another part of the dominion in order to earn a livelihood. Another large group is composed of students many of whom are from the rural areas of our nation. They are forced to go to the cities to attend university, technical school or vocational school in order to further their education. Up to the present time this large group of voters has been unable to cast

May 28, 1970
Canada Elections Act
a ballot in federal elections. Then there is the group of Canadians who travel for business or pleasure. They do not always know when the government wishes to call an election. These people often have made their plans and find that on voting day they are in another country or in another part of our country. These people also lose their opportunity to help choose the type of administration they feel should be running our country.
I am very concerned that we are to have a new Elections Act which will probably serve the Canadian nation for many years and yet the most effective measure to give votes to people in the classes I have mentioned is not contained in it. I refer, of course, to the absentee ballot. I come from the province of British Columbia which for a number of years has had the absentee ballot for provincial elections. I was a member of the provincial House in British Columbia before coming to Ottawa and I know the problems connected with absentee voting. I also know that tens of thousands of absentee ballots are cast by voters who are absent from their own poll but are still within their riding. Again, absentee ballots are cast by university students. These are students who come from areas in the interior of British Columbia. They are allowed to go to a poll in Vancouver and vote for a candidate representing a constituency in the interior. This is important to the students because on election day they would be unable to get back to their constituencies 500 or 600 miles away and cast their ballot.
Other provinces have an absentee voting system. I suggest that if provincial governments can devise such systems and make them work, such a system could also work on a federal basis. I do not suggest I am too happy about the type of enumeration we have in British Columbia, but again this is a matter of a change in a system which the federal government could easily bring about in an effort to see that more people are in a position to cast their ballots. I do not see anything wrong with someone from my constituency, whether he or she happens to be in Toronto, Ottawa, Winnipeg or Vancouver, going to a ballot-box and having the opportunity to cast an absentee ballot for one of the candidates running in my constituency. In this day of electronic gadgets which are in the process of being perfected to an ever-increasing degree, the tallying of absentee ballots should not be too difficult.

[DOT] (8:20 p.m.)
Might I point out that we have enumerated Canadians for a number of federal purposes. We have lists of Canadians for the Canada Pension Plan, for unemployment insurance, for family allowances and for a host of other things. Surely, with the talent we have scattered throughout the various government departments it should not be too difficult to establish an enumeration plan which we could handle from a central base, effectively and well. Such a system would extend the franchise to many more hundreds of thousands of Canadians and would give us that much more democracy in our nation.
I wish to deal briefly with the system which the government seems to think will take the place of an absentee ballot, namely, the proxy system of voting. I know we will be dealing with the clauses of the bill in committee but, Mr. Speaker, I hope you will allow me to spend a little time dealing with this system of voting as outlined in the bill. We find on page 117 of the bill the reference to a system of voting by proxy.
Proxy voting means that if someone is absent from his home riding, a certificate may be obtained and one individual may cast a ballot for that person. I do not like such a system. I think it can lead to a host of abuses. Just to point out one of the weaknesses in it, I wish to read part of the clause outlining the people who may vote by proxy. The three relevant paragraphs are:
(a)	his absence from the polling division in the course of his employment as a fisherman, mariner or prospector,
(b)	his illness or physical incapacity, or
(c)	his absence from the polling division while a full-time student duly registered at a recognized educational institution in Canada during an academic term.
May I return to the first paragraph-

III.	An effort should be made to increase public participation in politics, by broadening the base of political contributions through tax concessions to donors.
IV.	Costs of election campaigns should be reduced, by shortening the campaign period, by placing limitations on expenditures on mass media by candidates and parties, and by prohibiting the payment of poll workers on election day.
V.	Public confidence in political financing should be strengthened, by requiring candidates and parties to disclose their incomes and expenditures.
Our party has always been willing to open its books to the general public to disclose campaign contributions, and we would like the other parties to do the same:
VI.	A registry under the supervision of a registrar should be established to audit and publish the financial reports required, and to enforce the provisions of the proposed "Election and Political Finances Act".
VII.	Miscellaneous amendments to broadcasting legislation should be enacted to improve the political communications field.
The committee found that many of the very large corporations were making heavy contributions and a limited number of companies were supplying the larger amounts of cash for political campaigns. This is not good in a democratic country and it can and does lead to abuse. I urge members of all parties to read this report and I trust they will accept the seven points laid down by the committee which I believe to be very sound.
There are several other matters which merit attention, Mr. Speaker, but I felt I should deal only with the two most important, the one concerning absentee voting and the other the costs of elections. The other points which should be discussed can be dealt with when the bill is before the House at the committee stage. I hope we will have discussion on the sections dealing with proxy voting versus absentee voting at that time.

Mr. Speaker, this is a most important bill: the size of the bill indicates this. Seldom are we asked to deal with a bill containing 355 pages and with more than three score amendments that have already been recommended by the committee. It is difficult to cover all aspects of a bill like this in debate. I commend the committee for the tremendous work they have done in preparing the many amendments already incorporated in the bill. I know more amendments are yet to be made.
I was very interested in the problem raised by the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. 
Harding) when he spoke of the small percentage of Canadian electors who participate in any specific election. We are all concerned with this problem and I do not think anything we add to this bill will result in bringing a greater percentage of the qualified electors to the polls.
It is up to us to ensure that our electoral legislation is just and equitable and provides an opportunity for every Canadian to participate in an election. Provision must be made for people absent from their constituencies to have an opportunity to vote. In many ways this bill has improved the situation in making it possible for people to participate in an election. There are more vital matters, however. While agreeing with the major part of the bill and supporting the bill in general, I think there are a number of ways in which it can be improved. There are some weak points in the bill and in several areas it must be amended to provide a more equitable opportunity to electors.
The recommendation in the bill to lower the voting age to 18 has resulted from a great deal of discussion. When I first became a member of this House I was strongly in favour of encouraging younger people to participate in the processes of democracy. I felt that we should encourage responsibility at as early an age as possible, but in meetings with young people, particularly students, I soon came to understand that there was no pressure from that group in this regard. It is a rather interesting aspect of this suggestion of lowering the voting age that general voting patterns in provincial elections where the voting age has already been lowered have not really changed from those in previous elections.
[DOT] (8:40 p.m.)
I have wondered why our young people have not been stronger in their demands for a lower voting age. However, I think this provision to give them the vote at 18 is good because it will give our young people the chance to participate in political decisions. Young people these days know much more about politics than we did or people of previous generations. I look forward to seeing how they meet the challenge. I hope they will understand that we are giving them the opportunity in this legislation to become involved in the political process. This should make democracy more real to them.
In addition to the provision lowering the voting age, the bill also contains the welcome

Hear, hear!

If the principle of identifying the political affiliation of any candidate nominated for an election is acceptable, why should we not extend that right across-the-board to all candidates? Why should there be discrimination against an independent candidate? Very often independent candidates run. It seems to me that if we think it fair that the candidates of a large party are to have their party affiliation noted on the ballot, we ought to allow even those who are running as independent members to show they are independent. After all, many of them have

May 28, 1970
Canada Elections Act
been elected in the past. I therefore question the justice of the decision to include on the ballot the political affiliation of only some candidates. I urge that this right be extended across-the-board to all candidates, or eliminated altogether.
Something else that interests me extremely is the recommendation of the bill that would eliminate a special privilege that British subjects have enjoyed. Immigrants from other countries have not been extended that same privilege. I know that across the country there are many people who feel this is a further breaking down of traditions. However, it is interesting to note that Great Britain has already changed this situation for the electors of that country, and thus has eliminated the concept of a Commonwealth citizenship. I can understand the feeling of the many Canadians who believe that the right to vote should extend to all people in an equitable fashion rather than in one way for some and another way for others. While this may be a controversial point in some areas and there may be some justification in objecting to this, there is equity and justice in Bill C-215 in this regard.
[DOT] (8:50 p.m.)
One of the best ways to encourage people to participate in the process of electing their representatives to the various legislatures and to the House of Commons is to eliminate all those grey areas where people believe there is injustice in the regulations as they exist. There are several major ways in which the bill falls short. I am disappointed that the bill does not deal with several rather important changes that could have been brought about. The President of the Privy Council (Mr. Macdonald) stated that a special committee has been set up to deal with party finances.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Will be.

A special committee will be set up. I think this is good. I would be much more critical of the bill if this were not being done. I do not think that now is the time to deal with this subject at length. In this area, however, there is a very vital aspect which will tend to encourage people to realize that the voting process is just and that the political process represents democracy and is a reflection of the thinking of people in a fair way. Not only is it important that the question of political contributions be dealt with in an above-board manner so that people will know that patronage or influence is not being 
used in respect of political contributions, but it would be wise as well to make political contributions tax exempt. There is no reason why this should not be so.
I am strongly in favour of retaining the right to give a portion of our income to charitable and useful causes on a tax exempt basis. What more important cause could there be than the preservation of democracy? We should encourage our citizens to voluntarily contribute to the political process, not just during election years but every year. I am not just talking about individual citizens, but also corporate citizens. If there were facilities for income tax deduction as are now provided for contributions for charitable reasons, people would be encouraged considerably by knowing that we value the democratic process. Contributions would not pass under the table, but would be above-board. They would be recognized as a worth-while and a patriotic cause. The special committee that is to be set up will have a very important responsibility. I am glad it will be given the opportunity to properly discuss this matter and hold public hearings, with some change being brought about in this aspect of the electoral process.
The greatest omission of all in these recommendations is the failure of the legislation to establish a permanent voters' list. Many of the problems we have been and will be talking about in this debate would be eliminated if we had a permanent voters' list. There is the usual criticism relating to finances. I agree that the cost of a permanent voters' list is something to consider. It would obviously be more expensive than setting up a voters' list for each federal election. There is an aspect of the permanent voters' list which is far more extensive than just federal. I refer to the problem of enumeration every time there is a federal, provincial or municipal election. If the cost of enumeration at all levels were added together, I doubt that it would be greater than the cost of a permanent voters' list. The matter of absentee voting would be largely solved by a permanent voters' list. Where there is a permanent voters' list, each year there is an enumeration. Every voter carries his identification, including his picture. It has tremendous value in preventing double-voting which tends to take place in every election.
I have witnessed the permanent voters' list in operation in other countries. It is a far more efficient way of determining those who have a right to vote. It is a continuous process and is of benefit to provincial and municipal
May 28, 1970

governments as well as to the federal government. Another important aspect of a permanent voters' list is that it permits the shortening of the election campaign period. One of the reasons we in Canada require nearly two months is because nearly half that time is taken up with enumeration and preparation of the voters' lists. In Great Britain and other countries where the permanent voters' list is used, it is possible to have an election within four to five weeks from the time the election is called. We require eight weeks in Canada because it takes that length of time for the enumeration and preparation of the voters' lists. Further consideration should be given to this matter.
This bill does not adequately solve the problem of unsatisfactory participation with regard to the percentage of people concerned about the election process. This really cannot be changed through legislation unless there is compulsory voting. While compulsory voting seems to be effective in countries such as the Netherlands, I doubt if Canada is ready for compulsory voting at this time. If the electoral law could be improved in several additional areas, recognizing that a number of errors in the previous election laws have already been corrected, I think it would go a long way to convince people that they have a responsibility to vote and participate in an election.
To cover a bill such as this in debate requires a much longer time than is at our disposal. In closing, I wish to say that I support the bill. I recognize there are some areas where it could be strengthened. There are a few areas where there are omissions. Amendments will be proposed aimed at correcting some of these weak points and omissions. If that is done, we will be able to regard this as a good piece of legislation which the House can support. I do hope, however, that some of the weaker areas can be strengthened.

speakeroldname: Mr. A. D. Alkenbrack (Fronlenac-Lennox and Addington):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to take a long time with my remarks on Bill C-215, or to go into extreme detail on many of the issues covered by this document. As I was preparing my notes I made a quick calculation and found that if I were to deal for one minute with each page of this document I would have to speak for 355 minutes. Even on one of my very best days, Mr. Speaker, I would not entertain such a thought.
It is important to me, though, to be able to put my thoughts on record with respect to
Canada Elections Act
some of the points covered by the bill in which I have a special interest. In recent years there has been a noticeable tendency on the part of our young people to express their thoughts, and more often their displeasure, about what they call the older generation and often we find ourselves wondering why these same young people fail to recognize a basic truism with respect to the so-called generation gap. I am thinking, Mr. Speaker, of the simple and fundamental fact that yesterday we were their generation and that tomorrow they will be our generation.
This does not alter the fact that we should be cognizant of the expressions of our young people and we should be responsive to their appeals. But our response to their appeals should be carefully thought out and should be based on reasonable premises. Mr. Speaker, I cannot think of a more reasonable response to our young people than to put them where the action is and allow them to express their thoughts and their wishes where it counts most, in the polling booth.
I know that many people have recoiled in horror at the thought of giving radical young people the right to vote for Members of Parliament. We are told that the majority of young people are leftist, that they are communists and everything else that is inimical to our way of life and government. But I do not believe those arguments. I believe in the integrity of our young people and I believe that when the chips are down the majority of young voters will elect to preserve our way of government for themselves and for their children. In other words, I am saying that I am in favour of giving our 18-year old citizens the right to vote in federal elections.
We hear from every side that our young people want the right to decide their own destinies and to determine who shall represent them in their government. We have an opportunity here, Mr. Speaker, to put those people to the test and let them play an active part in the affairs of state. What they do with the franchise is up to them, but at least we should make it available to them.
I am opposed, however, to lowering the age limit to 18 for those who stand for public office. I do not agree we have to go that far to show our young people that we are with them and that we think it is time for them to become active in government. No man or woman who has just reached the age of 18 has had a chance to receive either a full education or an appreciable degree of practical experience. Education and practical experi-

May 28, 1970
Canada Elections Act
ence cannot be given to any 18-year old the day alter an election in order to fit that person for a public office which he or she might have won at the polls. For very practical reasons, then, I must oppose reducing the age limit for standing for public office. I am making every effort to qualify my criticisms because I am most anxious to reach conciliation with the government members and speed this important volume of revisions to our electoral laws through this House. I am making an effort to be constructive and helpful.
It has come to my attention since Bill C-215 was tabled that the electoral office has mailed out questionnaires to returning officers in all federal ridings across the country to elicit their comments and suggestions as to how our electoral laws and practices might be improved. I have been informed that many of the returning officers have suggested that the three-day training period for returning officers is not long enough to be effective. On the basis of information I have gathered, I would suggest that the training period should be lengthened to one week. Nothing is to be lost by making such a change, Mr. Speaker, but we do stand to gain a great deal in improved efficiency and morale.
I have also learned that most of those questioned feel that the general content of the training course is sufficient with respect to administrative and financial matters but, as I have mentioned, the time period is not long enough. I would like to make a suggestion here with respect to the financial rewards given to returning officers in the discharge of their duties. In the first place, Mr. Speaker, these could hardly be referred to as financial rewards. It is my impression that payments to returning officers during the performance of their duties are scarcely sufficient to cover their expenses. It has also been brought to my attention that returning officers receive no honorarium or other financial assistance between elections. I suggest we consider paying some form of retainer to returning officers between elections. In this way we can compensate them for actual expenses incurred and also compensate them for their diligence and even their availability. It scarcely needs to be mentioned that we could not hold an election without the services of efficient and devoted returning officers.
Another point which I feel should be dealt with while I am on the subject of returning officers is the time alloted to them in which to finalize the appointment of enumerators. It is

my opinion that insufficient time is allowed. This is especially true in the case of rural ridings, Mr. Speaker, and I think we should have a close look at this aspect of returning officers' duties. It is the enumerator who provides the information from which the voters' rolls are compiled, and I cannot emphasize too strongly the importance of this phase of the election process.
I should like to turn, now, to some of the suggestions for amendments which have been made, in this case some of the items mentioned in Appendix A which is attached to the report of the committee. For example, it is recommended that with prior approval of the Chief Electoral Officer, for good and valid reason the returning officer may authorize the amalgamation of two or more polling divisions. The recommendations speaks of "two or more". I recommend that the number be limited to two only. This limitation would avoid too great a degree of centralization and the confusion which would result from the amalgamation of a number of divisions in one premise.
[DOT] (9:10 p.m.)
In many rural polling divisions and subdivisions there is no longer a post office in which to display notices of proclamations. Section 22 deals with the sending of proclamations to postmasters at post offices. Due to the closing of many post offices in rural areas of Canada by the Postmaster General (Mr. Kierans), we will be unable to send out proclamations in the usual way to the electors in rural areas. Several townships in the northern part of my riding have no post offices at all in which they can post these proclamations. The question that follows is: Where are we going legally to post these proclamations? This is the question the committee of the whole will have to deal with, and the matter will have to be resolved before final passage of this bill.
I see another problem in section 24, which provides, among other things, that the revising officers are authorized to take names off a preliminary list of electors on the request of the persons themselves to remove their names from the list. I claim that no names should be allowed to be taken off any list of eligible voters, regardless of the wishes of the persons named or any personal request that is made. On the contrary, if a request is made to remove a name from the list, it might be made by a radical or changeable sort of person who would afterwards complain at
May 28. 1970

what had been done. I submit that once the names are put on the list, if they are there legitimately, under no circumstances should we go to the expense and bother of removing them.
I also disagree with the provisions of section 29. I suggest this amendment is discriminatory. It refers to the now infamous limit of 75 nominations for recognition of a political party. If this bill passes, parties must have 75 officially nominated and registered candidates to be recognized as a party by the party name on the ballot. What about the case where a party could nominate only 74 candidates, which is possible? After all, you cannot force people to be candidates. Such a party would certainly be entitled to a measure of electoral recognition on the ballot in proportion to the parties that nominate 75 candidates or more. So you can see, Mr. Speaker, how ludicrous is this Liberal-loaded dispensation of so-called justice from the sponsors of the just society.
It has been suggested to me that this provision requiring any new party to have 75 official nominations is the new Liberal method of fighting separatism. This figure of 75 is one seat more than the present federal electoral potential in the province of Quebec. If this is the government's strategy, I say they will never fight separatism successfully. It cannot be fought by discrimination, by making two classes of federal candidate, one with the blessing of the government and the party name alongside that of the candidate, the other an electoral martyr with no party affiliation indicated on the same ballot. If it ever does become necessary to fight separatism, it must be fought out in the open on the hustings with no electoral discrimination against any party or its candidates.
I next have some brief remarks to make on section 39, which provides for the setting up of a system of proxy voting. I am not condemning this system completely; it may be all right. Some day we may be able to work out a good system of proxy voting. But we must be very careful to check into it, on the ground that it is open to abuse. For example, someone might take advantage of the absence of a neighbour to vote twice. Section 42 provides that the political affiliation of a candidate who is endorsed by the leader of a registered party or his designated representative will be printed on the ballot paper. Section 43 provides that the requirement to indicate the address and occupation of a candidate on the ballot paper will be dispensed with. Basically,
Canada Elections Act
I am against any change being made to the nature of the ballot. This amendment takes away much of a candidate's individualism from the electoral process. I am sure most members in this chamber depend on individualism more than anything else to get themselves elected. If this amendment carries, future candidates will no longer have the benefit of any local or constituency identification as part of their individualism.
For example, a non-resident candidate could be parachuted into a riding, as was done by the Liberal party in the constituency that I represent, in the last election in June, 1968. Such a candidate would not require any identification on the ballot and would suddenly and legitimately be in the business of votegetting. Although I realize that this can be argued both ways, I am putting the case against the non-resident, parachuted candidate.
Why the sudden electoral recognition of political parties? The Liberals say they are now going to put the name of the political party on the ballot. Since Trudeaumania is dying, the designation "Liberal" will be nothing but a millstone around the necks of future candidates for the Liberal Party.
Oh, oh!

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Then you should be in favour of it.

I thank hon. members for their response, though I well understand why they are concerned. Generally speaking, do we members of this House so much lack the attributes of individuality as public servants that we have to have the crutch of the name of a political party alongside our own name on the ballot in order to get elected? I think not.
Our seats in this House are not marked with the names of parties. There is the name of the elected member only; no political affiliation is stated, not even the member's riding. This designation is correctly unbiased. We are permitted as individuals, by the combined electoral decision of the people of Canada in their might and indeed in their majesty, to speak in this House when recognized by you, Mr. Speaker, and to exercise our vote when asked to and permitted to do so. I am against any and all political parties getting a free ride on the ballot paper. The name of the individual candidate is sufficient identification. This has always proven true in the past and will suffice for the future.

May 28, 1970
Canada Elections Act
The indication of a candidate's address and occupation has always been useful information. The ballot showed whether the candidate was a farmer, a merchant or even a hockey player. If a candidate is running, for example, in Marshy Hope, Nova Scotia, and he lives in Kinbasket Lake, British Columbia-two places at the extreme ends of this country that I have visited and which greatly enthralled me-the voters in Nova Scotia are entitled to have knowledge of his domicile on the ballot. I am sure you will agree with me, Mr. Speaker, that any amendment such as this will not serve the electors of Canada. Any such amendment would be a gross and arrogant disservice to the electors of Canada. It would also be a disservice in respect of the type of information they have been able to expect on the ballot since the time of Confederation but which apparently now is to be eliminated.
[DOT] (9:20 p.m.)
The outlets for the sale of alcoholic beverages are to be closed on an ordinary polling day only while the polls are open. I am in complete agreement with this amendment which requires that all the outlets for the sale of alcohol be closed only while the polls are open. The former practice was that they were closed for the complete 24-hour period. I do not think that is necessary any more because we have a better informed and more considerate electorate than we had many years ago.
I will drink to that.

Amendment 52 states
that any form of tampering with the election material or campaign literature of a candidate is an offence. However, this amendment is without power or authority. Clause 73 states:
Every one who without authority, takes down, removes, covers up, mutilates, defaces or alters any printed advertisement, placard, poster or banner having reference to the election of a candidate is guilty of an offence against this act.
This clause has no power. It applies principally to roadside advertising, tree and pole signs, and so on. This type of advertising is put up and remains there only at the pleasure of the public. It is not completely lawful for anyone to put up a sign on or within the right-of-way of any public road. All public roads in Canada, except the beautiful and presently tulip-lined driveways in Ottawa, are within the jurisdiction of either the provinces or municipalities. Moreover, it is against the laws of hydro and telephone companies to

erect signs on hydro and telephone poles. The federal government, however, can convict no one of contravening clause 73 of this bill in respect of the removal of signs on roadways. Mr. Speaker, that is all I have to say at this time. I hope to place the remainder of my comments on the record during the debate at committee of the whole stage. We have not had such a debate for some time, and I shall look forward to the debate on this bill in committee of the whole.

Mr. Speaker, on entering this debate I should like to congratulate the members of the committee who assisted in putting together such a substantial number of amendments to the Elections Act which in the end will achieve what all Members of Parliament must desire, that is, making available as far as possible the franchise to every Canadian over 18 years of age. The objectives contained in the amendments will be discussed in detail during the committee stage of the bill.
At this time I should like to talk about some omissions from the bill which, had they been incorporated, in my opinion at least would have guaranteed the franchise to a great many more Canadians. The first item I should like to mention is the permanent voting roll. It is called by a number of different names in different places, but at least under this system every elector would have his name on a roll. This would mean, as is the case in Great Britain at the present time, that an election could be called and a vote taken in a very short period of time. I hope this system will be provided in the Elections Act in the days ahead.
I hoped the committee would take such a step. I realize it is a very expensive move, but once such a move has been made the system is established. No longer would there be the severe problems which face many Canadians who are disqualified from voting because they happen to be located in a constituency other than the one in which they resided at the time the writ was issued. I find it very difficult to explain to an elector why his name is not on the voters' list. I find it difficult to explain to him why he cannot vote. In my view this is a much more serious matter than almost anything else. I am certain that thousands of Canadians are deprived of the right to vote because we do not have a permanent roll. I realize it is difficult to establish such a system, but it must be done some day and I ask: Why should we not face up to it today,
May 28, 1970

rather than putting it off until a future Parliament finds it must undertake the task? Unless we do this now, many Canadians at the next general election will discover they are deprived of their vote.
The other subject on which I should like to spend a little time relates to another bill which I hope the Government House Leader will consider referring to a committee. If he does not do so, I shall endeavour to propose an amendment at the proper time in respect of this bill. I believe, however, that it warrants the consideration of a committee of this House designated by the government. I refer to Bill C-211, relating to polls. I do not have any objection to polls being prepared and used in any shape or form by political parties at any time. I do not object to their being used at election time if proper guidelines are associated with them. What concerns me greatly, however-and I have observed this situation in six elections-is that there are no guidelines. Polls can be misused and therefore can be very dangerous.
I introduced Bill C-211, not because I am opposed to polls as such but because I am opposed to them in the context of politics today when there are no guidelines in this respect. I believe they pose a danger to the Canadian public and also to the credibility of the news media. I say this because during the recent election in the province of Quebec, polls were used first by the French newspapers and then by the two English speaking dailies in the city of Montreal.
[DOT] (9:30 p.m.)
As far as I am concerned, they were used to do nothing more than stampede the electorate, especially the uncommitted electors, to the Liberal party. Liberals in that province might rejoice in that fact. As a matter of fact, I think the result in the province of Quebec on election night was something for all Canadians to rejoice in, because at least it gave them four more years in which to prepare for the next onslaught by the separatist party in that province. But what concerns me is that the polls that were produced had no more association with the facts and the reality on election day than the man in the moon. It was quite obvious that the polls, in combination with the business community and its great Brinks operation, were used to stampede and frighten the electorate into voting for the Liberal party. That frightens me, Mr. Speaker, because while it was for the benefit of Canada that time, it may well turn out at
Canada Elections Act
some future time that individuals in powerful places may try to manipulate and frighten the electorate in a way which may not be good for Canada. That is why I introduced my bill.
I feel that all too often in this country polls are being used for the benefit of a political party. It does not always happen to be the Liberal party that is using them, but I say that people who are subjected to polls that later prove to be inaccurate, sometimes gravely inaccurate, not only lose respect for the organization or group using the polls but lose respect for the media generally and lose confidence in what the media place before them. As a result, these polls are dangerous.
On the other hand, I believe there are good polls, produced by organizations that take a great deal of care, that have a formula or guideline that they rigidly follow because they have respect for their own reputations. I believe the Gallup poll is one such poll. There are few people who would argue against it, considering its history. But when you find a man who holds himself out to be a political analyst carrying out a poll with a base of 800 or so people, to cover 6 million or 7 million people, you can have little respect for that poll especially when it includes 35 per cent uncommitted voters. In order to protect the public we have to do one of two things. We must either lay down some guidelines or ban the public use of polls during an election campaign. I have no objection to polls being used by political parties for their own internal purposes, but I take strong exception to their being used to dupe the public.
Our television media in particular must give serious consideration to the way they use polls at election time. Referring again to the recent CBC coverage of the Quebec election, I remember the start of its coverage on election night, when the program included Norman Depoe, Charles Lynch and another commentator whose name I forget. They began by saying that in all likelihood a minority government would be elected that night. Even they were fooled by the polls, and as the wave of Liberal victories started coming in they began to back off and back off. This is what polls do. They are put before the public as facts and the public accepts them as the gospel.
When you get so-called experts like Depoe and Lynch repeating what the polls have said, polls based on a sampling of 800 people and including 35 per cent uncommitted voters, I object to this. This is what we have to be concerned about. You and I, Mr. Speaker,

May 28, 1970
Canada Elections Act
read the papers a lot. We know their political background; we know the political background of news. But the general public does not know this background, does not read the newspapers as carefully as we do and at election time places great dependence on what newspapers have to say. If the newspapers tell them, as in the recent Quebec election, that there will be a minority government, that the separatist party is coming on like a house on fire, that there is a great danger it will elect the largest group of members, the public must become very concerned. In that election campaign the polls and the business community combined. Business firms lined up the Brinks trucks, loaded them up with so-called company assets and started them on their way to the Ontario border.
You and I, Mr. Speaker, are intelligent enough to know that it did not make any difference whether those Brinks trucks stayed in Montreal, whether the paper assets stayed in the vaults or whether the trucks crossed the border and went on to Toronto, but unfortunately a great many unknowing people in Quebec were frightened to death and, so far as I am concerned, were deceived into voting for the Liberal party because the newspapers and the business community joined together to commit a fraud on them. As I have already said, I did not mind this in that election. I was quite happy to see the Liberal party roll to the victory it achieved, and not being a Liberal that is a fairly big concession for me to make, but I am frightened that this fraud could be perpetrated on the public at some future date when it was not in the public interest. As Members of Parliament we should be concerned to see that when polls are used in an election campaign a set of rules or guidelines will be followed to assure that to some degree the information given is authentic.
[DOT] (9:40 p.m.)
Mr. Speaker, I believe that the main objective of all members of the House of Commons should be to see that every elector over 18 years of age in this country, after this bill passes, has the right to vote. I believe that even at the great cost involved in producing a permanent roll we should move amendments to this bill to indicate to the Chief Electoral Officer that immediate steps should be taken to produce a permanent roll. We should not be concerned in the future about the disqualification of Canadian citizens from voting-because they did not happen to be in the [Mr. Coates.J
electoral district on the date the writ was issued, were not enumerated, did not realize their name was not on the list or did not discover the omission in time to have it placed on the list. These are the two matters that give me greatest concern.

Mr. Speaker, I will keep my remarks brief because I know that my good friend, the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Gilbert), has something stirring and brilliant to say that we will all want to hear. I shall keep my eye on the clock and give him some time.
Much has been said about the thickness of this bill, but to be fair it should be pointed out that the former Elections Act was almost as thick. We should devote ourselves to the very good changes that have been made to it. The first change that all members are expected to comment on and to be in favour of is giving the vote to 18-year olds. I doubt if many politicians in Canada will say they are against this proposition. I think we say we are in favour of it, despite what the cynics might feel, because of the arguments which have been presented in a non-partisan way to the effect that the young people of today are better educated and better informed, thanks to the mass media and to instant communication systems. Recently some children from Quebec came to my city of Sarnia, and I doubt very much whether such an experiment would have been tried 10 or even 15 years ago. What pleases me more than the fact that the 18-year old is to get the vote is that we have gone all the way and indicated: We are going to trust you with the responsibility of governing this country.
I know that some people genuinely feel that this is going too far. This thought has been sincerely expressed in this House tonight. But I would remind the hon. gentleman and those who object to this proposal that in 1939 we gave a much greater responsibility to our 18-year olds. We put them in charge of $6 million aircraft, we put them in charge of platoons and in charge of ships. They had the ability to make decisions whether someone should live or die. We gave them a greater responsibility than this bill is giving them by suggesting that they stand for election to this House.
The second matter on which I should like to comment is the permanent voters' list. When I first came to this House of Commons I thought there was much to commend a permanent voters' list. I have spent some time
May 28. 1970

studying with a constituent of mine, Mr. John McEachran, who served as secretary to the Barbeau Commission, because I knew he had devoted a great amount of study to it. There is much to commend it and that is why it is in the politically grey area; that is why politicians can argue fervently on one side or the other without being too far off base.
What politician or individual who has participated in a political campaign cannot see the benefit of shorter political campaigns? They cost less money, it is easier on the candidate and it is much easier on the individual who has already been elected and is well known in his constituency. He has a definite advantage When he goes back to his riding to oppose someone not so well known. When we look at the disadvantages we must consider the fact that it has already been tried. In his remarks the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Macdonald) commented on the bill which was scrapped in 1934. Even in 1934 the Canadian population was so mobile that this system would not work. I wonder about the mobility of our population today, those who live in the cities and, perhaps even more so, those who live in the rural communities. I know that within two years of leaving Sarnia when I went back to the service club to which I belonged, which formerly had 45 members, there were only eight. The remainder had moved out of the community. This is typical of Canada and I think it is one of the things that makes the country great-we do not think that we must settle in one particular area. Unfortunately, this situation defeats one of the benefits of having a permanent voters' list.
In Canada we have the expertise, the ladies who go around and do the enumerating. Greater than all the proclamations put in all the post offices across Canada is the fact that people are knocking on every door reminding us that there is an election. I think there is something to commend this approach. We have heard that Americans who have studied our system say that perhaps in the long run it is not so bad; that in fact it is better than theirs. Coming from an American, that is quite an admission.
I like the party affiliation on the ballot because the House of Commons and our democratic system operates on the party system. Finally, after all these years, we are going to recognize that fact. I do not think it is a question of feeling that you cannot stand on your own merits, that people might not
Canada Elections Act
know you. You won as a member of a party and if your party is elected it is the one that will govern. I think the suggestion that we have the party name on the ballot is commendable. I am sorry that one hon. member indicated it might be something the Liberal Party was doing in order to prevent separatism in Quebec.
I suggest there is nothing magic about the number 75. Perhaps there could be a saw-off at 50, but I think there is something to commend setting a certain number so that we will not get a frivolous or vexatious type of candidate. As a Liberal, of course I am particularly proud of my party and proud to have that connotation opposite my name on the ballot.
Who is to vote? We have already commented on the 18-year olds. We have already commented on the fact that British subjects who voted at the last election shall have the right to vote. I am rather sorry that we did not go one step further and recognize that there are in Canada some citizens who have not obtained Canadian citizen status. Some of them have been here for many years, some only for a few years; but they are making their living here. They pay land and other taxes here, have their children educated here, pay income tax and do their job. I wonder if there is not some way in which we can give these people the vote, because I think there is a grain of discrimination when we say, "You pay your taxes, but the British subjects and Canadian citizens will decide how your tax money is to be spent." I like the idea of proxy voting, though I would have preferred some system of mailing ballots. I prefer the secret ballot where only the voter knows how he has voted.
The act points out the benefits of majority government. A majority government has time to look at the hundreds of sections in these acts. This is a very important issue because, as you know, our party stands for the abolition of the Senate. But I am a pragmatist and at times I am flexible. I think we should have an elected rather than an appointed Senate. This would be at least a first step in developing more democratic institutions in this country.
One wonders what are the qualifications of a Senator. First of all, he must reach the grand old age of 60, 65 or 70. He must be a member of one of the two major political parties. If he has made his contributions to the party in time, effort and money over the years he is rewarded with the high honour of being appointed a Senator. They have a committee to study the news media, and now that

maintopic: GRAIN-PROVISION OF FREIGHT CARS FOR SPECIAL DELIVERY PERMIT WHEAT
GRAIN-PROVISION OF FREIGHT CARS FOR SPECIAL DELIVERY PERMIT WHEAT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on May 7 I directed this question to the Minister without Portfolio (Mr. Lang) in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board, as reported at page 6676 of Hansard:
In view of the fact that many of the delivery points still at the lowest quota levels are points which were unable to deliver a five-bushel quota last year and in respect of which provision was made for special delivery permits, may I ask whether provision is to be made for extra cars to take account of deliveries on special delivery permits?
The minister answered:
The grain to be delivered under special delivery permits is not treated differently from grain deliveries under other quotas.
[DOT] (10:00 p.m.)
He went on to state:
A purpose of the block system is to ensure in due course an equal opportunity for delivery as
May 28. 1970

Proceedings on Adjournment Motion far as possible. Often it is the individual elevator companies which decide which particular elevator within their ownership should receive cars ahead of others; responsibility often rests with them.
This situation first developed on July 30 when an announcement was made by the Canadian Wheat Board that special permits would be issued to farmers who were unable to deliver a five-bushel quota prior to the end of the last crop, that a special delivery permit would be granted up to a maximum of one bushel per specified acre and that there would be no deadline for applications. I agree with the principle involved in these special delivery permits. However, as the winter season wore on it became evident that much grain had not yet been delivered under the special delivery permits because of lack of space in country elevators. On February 9 last there were still 388 elevator delivery points in Saskatchewan which were on the unit delivery quota, while 567 points were handled on a one-bushel quota in that province. The tight delivery situation still prevails.
The minister has repeatedly said in the House of Commons that no provision was to be made for cars to handle shipments under these special delivery permits. He said that the block system would handle the situation. This would be rather difficult to do because the block system was only introduced during the current crop year. On April 13 there were still 22 delivery points in Saskatchewan on the unit quota, and 31 points in the province of Manitoba. I suggest that it is a very hollow policy to make provision for special delivery permits for farmers who could not deliver five bushels per acre in the crop year, while at the same time making no provision for the movement of that grain once it had been delivered or to allow for the movement of grain to create space for these special deliveries. This situation would have been remedied by an allocation of cars based on the special delivery permit applications. Since there was a deadline for those applications, this would have been possible.
The minister now says it will be possible to deliver four bushels per acre during the current crop year on current wheat deliveries. I hope that this extension includes full provision for the special delivery permits which were allowed. The block system of movement referred to by the minister in his answer has brought about some improvement. However, the absence of help for those points which have special delivery permits complicated the 
grain movement picture during the past year. The block system does not solve all the problems of grain movement. With respect to the provision of cars for movement, there have been reports that the railways were pulling cars out of grain movement last year. From time to time the Canadian Wheat Board has made requests for cars from the railways for particular blocks, and the railways have not been able to supply those cars. This does not show up in the figures of grain movement and the figures of cars made available to elevator points.
The minister says that elevator companies allocate cars to the specific delivery points within the block. This is true. However, on February 9 I obtained a report of all delivery points in the quota system as of that date. There were entire lines which were still on the unit quota. Most of those were CPR points. On February 9, over 230 of 388 delivery points of the unit quota were CPR points. In addition, there were a number of points on the unit quota where there were both CPR and CNR facilities. On April 13, there were 22 points in Saskatchewan still on the unit quota. Every one of them was on a CPR line. I suggest that the CPR has not done its job. A good deal of the difficulties have been with respect to the CPR points.
I trust that the minister will take the situation with respect to special delivery permits into account and ensure that there is an equitable delivery situation as of the end of the current crop year. I hope that action will begin shortly which will ensure that enough cars are allocated to those elevator points which were unable to handle five bushels per acre last year and for which special delivery permits were issued during the current crop year.

Mr. Speaker, in following up his question of May 7, the hon. member for Regina East (Mr. Burton) has confirmed what I suspected when the original question was asked. He seems to be under some misapprehension about the way in which the deferred delivery permits work. As far as delivery opportunity is concerned, they were an entitlement to individual producers to deliver as space was available. This meant that as space became available in the Prairie region the deferred delivery permits could be used by individual producers for the delivery of grain.
As the hon. member knows, the unit quota has been delivered in all points, all points are
May 28. 1970	COMMONS
now on at least a one-bushel quota and a rapid movement upward is occurring. At that stage with the delivery of unit quotas there should be no particular reason for any lack of opportunity for producers to deliver on their deferred delivery permits. Of course, with the deferred delivery permits really being treated in the same way as any other delivery opportunity, the programming of cars for the collecting of grain automatically takes care of the situation of having cars available for these particular delivery opportunities. The hon. member asks whether the four-bushel quota delivered during this crop year includes the deferred deliveries, and of course it does. Deferred delivery means that less grain can be taken into the system this year than might otherwise have been taken in under quotas this year because, of course, the deferred delivery amounts are included in this year's deliveries.
As I indicated in the House today again, a very rapid increase in the number of cars and in the movement of grain in Thunder Bay has taken place, a constant position is being fairly well maintained for Vancouver throughout the period, and a very high figure, something like 10,000 cars per week, are expected to be loaded in the Prairie region for both directions now and in the months immediately ahead. This will mean one of the record movements of grain out of the Prairie region compared with any similar period in the past. It is a movement not only of wheat to meet the very many sales demands which have accumulated for this period, but also to meet the need for moving the balance of the rape-seed crop and the very heavy barley shipments in response to demands which have occurred for this part of the year and on into the next crop year. All in all, the movement of grain will be extremely rapid and the hon. member for Regina East has really no need to worry further about the specific delivery opportunity to which he referred.

The questions to which I shall refer at this time are those which I put to the minister on May 6, 1970, as reported in Hansard at page 7326. They are on the subject of trade, particularly in crude petroleum and natural gas

Is the minister ready to forget his umbrage with the United States and get down to the hard bargaining necessary to ensure accelerated trade in our surplus crude petroleum and natural gas ... and thereby stimulate the employment of our young Canadians, graduates and undergraduates?
A person has only to drive along the Trans-Canada Highway to see young men and women from our colleges and universities thumbing rides from passing motorists just as people used to ride the rods in the thirties looking for employment. Let us get down to brass tacks. The present government signed an agreement with the United States, a secret agreement that I flushed out about a year or a year and a half ago in the committee, in which Canada agreed with the United States on certain quotas with respect to the export of crude petroleum. It was agreed at that time that the United States had the privilege to act unilaterally, and this I objected to.
If you look at the line of questioning I have directed on this subject over the last two or three years, particularly during the last few months, you will find I suggested that the government erred when they entered into that secret agreement. Nevertheless, it was entered into.
The minister has switched positions during the last month or two, and this puts me in mind of the position taken by Molotov and Von Papen who switched positions when Germany, having made a secret agreement wih Russia, a non-aggression pact, only a short time later marched into Russia. Because the minister feels it will be popular with university students and the young people who are now going to vote at 18, he has switched positions and come up with an anti-American policy that is good for home consumption but poor for trade and employment.
What happened today as a result of the minister's speech at Denver? If the minister was a responsible minister, a man steeped in the knowledge of diplomacy, he would not go down to a small place like Denver and insult
May 28, 1970

Proceedings on Adjournment Motion the United States; he would go to Washington and do some hard bargaining in confidence over the conference table, using the kind of diplomacy that brings confidence and respect between two nations. The press gallery in Ottawa had a report from the White House today, and it could not be more timely. This is what the president and his cabinet have now said about Canada, because of this childish diplomacy on the part of the minister:
Herewith excerpt from White House ... re Canadian oil imports.
In our view these imports create at least an indirect threat to the national security for two reasons.
It goes on to say what the reasons are. I do not have time to read them into the record, but they cut back further on exports of crude petroleum from Canada to the United States. Through the actions of this government, not only its antagonism of the United States, as with Great Britain and France, but its tax threat, and the fear that hangs over the extractive industries like an umbrella, we have now lost $62 million in oil revenue in the province of Alberta. What did the minister say? I wish the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) would take him more seriously, but maybe he takes him as seriously as the United States took this speech which took two hours to deliver. On one of the many pages in his speech he said:
In particular, I cannot see that it-
Meaning Canada.
-would legislate a tax climate in which the Canadian petroleum industry would be put at any significantly increased disadvantage compared with the industry in the U.S.
I think the white paper is going to be rammed through, with a few innocuous things having been withdrawn. But it has killed the confidence not only of Canadians but of foreign investors. Because of the expense involved the extractive industries have to attract foreign investment. I am a Canadian but I am practical and realistic enough to know that if you eliminate United States' investment in this country, as I said before, it will be like pulling the plug out of the bathtub-you will watch the water go down. There will be unemployment everywhere, and there is 8 per cent now as a result of the actions of the present government. It is a strange thing, but although the White House said today that Canada's government has undermined the security of the United States by its national oil policy, this policy was established by the Conservative government led by the right hon.

gentleman from Prince Albert (Mr. Diefen-baker) which at that time had the confidence of the United States.
It is strange when we think that we establish the national oil policy and today import from Venezuela $200 million more crude petroleum than we export. We in western Canada are now using only 40 per cent of our possible production either through export or domestically. The answer is that we are about to become involved in a trade war with the United States when approximately 8 per cent of our labour force, when we consider the students, is unemployed, when we have the biggest crash in the stock-market since 1930 and when we have this childish diplomacy going on which is ruining the markets. As if it were not enough for the Minister without Portfolio (Mr. Lang) and other ministers to lose our wheat markets, now they are trying hard to lose the western Canada oil and gas markets.

VETERANS AFFAIRS-INTERIM INCREASE IN PENSIONS AND ALLOWANCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to see the minister here tonight. I expect that next week will be an uncomfortable time for him, when one considers that the 23rd Dominion Convention of the Canadian Legion is to meet in Ottawa and the minister is scheduled to speak, I believe on Monday.
[DOT] (10:20 p.m.)
Essentially, Mr. Speaker, I asked the minister today whether, in view of the Canadian Legion convention being held here in Ottawa, he planned to announce any special interim benefits to that convention, because all members of the House realize but do not necessarily accept the fact that the Woods report recommendations will take a great deal of time before they are implemented. I asked my question about special interim benefits but the minister remained rooted in his seat in dumb silence. I asked my question about special interim benefits because there is a tragic need for disability pensions and war veterans allowances to be raised immediately because of the spiralling costs of living. But the minister did not respond today. I asked my question about special interim benefits because ever since the Woods task force was announced the veterans have been led to
DEBATES	7473
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion believe that the government really did care about their sacrifices and was going to do something. But the minister said nothing today.
I wonder how many veterans in need realize that the terms of reference of the Woods report did not allow the commission to consider the war veterans allowances nor the amount of the disability benefits at all. The thing that is vital to veterans' welfare, namely money, was completely excluded from the review of the Canada Pension Act. What good is tidying up the administration and making a big noise about it, and misleading the veterans to expect an increase? Some four years ago the government initiated a comprehensive review of veterans pension problems and published 148 findings and recommendations in a document which became known as the Woods report. This report was greeted with great hope and enthusiasm by veterans and their organizations throughout the land. At last, they said, Canada is going to right some of the past wrongs which condemned many who had served in our armed services to live in poverty, indignity and embarrassment.
During the intervening four years the problems for hundreds of veterans were solved forever-they simply died. The longer we await improvements to the Canada Pension Plan, the more problems will be solved in the same way. In spite of a year's excellent work by the Standing Committee, no action is contemplated by the government at least until the white paper on social security is tabled next fall. And the lethargic, legislative process could easily drag this matter out for another year. Contrast this, if you will, with the speed with which Members of Parliament raised their own pensions. The job was done in about two weeks.
I think the ex-military should become militant once more and demand an interim raise immediately. The Canadian Legion meets next week for its national convention. I hope it takes strong action. I know the minister is going to say, among other things, that nothing can be done until the government review of the whole fabric of social legislation is complete. He will probably restate the half billion dollar figure which he cited today, which he said the government gave him but which in fact is the statutory amount given not by the government but by Parliament. I wonder if the minister was not unintentionally misleading us today because this $500 million, while it is larger than in previous years, is the result of more people becoming eligible.

But the fact remains-and neither the minister nor the government can escape it-that many veterans desperately need a raise in both the disability and allowance benefits. The basic rate can be raised without amending anything and we do not need to wait for legislation on the Woods report. I urge the minister to fight for the veterans and to fight his colleagues on the treasury benches if necessary. The flim-flam has gone on long enough. The veterans need a raise now, and I hope the minister announces it next week.

reason that the hon. member himself has just stated. The government at the present time is reviewing the total fabric of social legislation. I share the interest, concern and sympathy of the hon. member for Fraser Valley West (Mr. Rose) in the cause of the veterans. On many occasions, in 1964, in 1966 and again in 1968 this government has shown concern by repeatedly increasing war veterans pensions.
